2027-05-02.title: Sixth Sunday of Resurrection
2027-05-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: How beautiful are the feet of the messenger
That they may all be one
2027-05-02.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The calendar notes that the feast of the Ascension of our Lord falls on the coming Thursday, 6 May, a day of obligation. Longer forms in the calendar: Isaiah 51:9–11 with 52:7–12; Acts 10:1–16; Ephesians 2:4–22; John 17:1–26. St Athanasius (2 May) gives way to the Sunday (verify locally). In the Latin calendar, the Sixth Sunday of Easter.
2027-05-02.verse: that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
theo: The Sixth Sunday of Resurrection stands at a threshold. On Thursday the Church will celebrate the Ascension of the Lord, and the readings of this Sunday already have the sound of a farewell and a sending. The first reading is a cry of joy from the prophet who comforted Israel in exile: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’” The watchmen on the ruined walls of Jerusalem see the Lord coming home, and the ruins themselves are told to sing: “Break forth together into singing, you ruins of Jerusalem; for the Lord has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.” Then a promise that reaches far beyond one city: “The Lord has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.” Paul hears in this text the vocation of every preacher of the Gospel: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Romans 10:15). The feet of the apostles were dusty and tired; one pair of them, the Church in India believes, walked the coast of Malabar. On this Sunday we give thanks for every messenger who brought the good news to us, and we remember that our own feet are meant for the same road.

The Acts of the Apostles shows how far that road would go. Peter is praying on a rooftop at Joppa around noon. He is hungry, and in a trance he sees “the heaven opened and something like a large sheet coming down, being lowered to the ground by its four corners”, full of animals that the Law of Moses forbade him to eat. A voice says, “Get up, Peter; kill and eat.” Peter answers as a faithful Jew who has kept the commandments all his life: “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is profane or unclean.” And the voice replies, “What God has made clean, you must not call profane.” Three times this happens. Peter does not yet understand, but at that very moment messengers from a Roman centurion named Cornelius are at the gate. The vision is not mainly about food; it is about people. Soon Peter will stand in a Gentile house and say, “I truly understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35). Notice how gently God leads his apostle. Peter's hesitation came from love of God's Law, not from hatred; God opens his heart step by step. The Church has never ceased to honour the people of Israel, from whom Peter, Mary and Jesus himself came; “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). What the vision opens is the door of that same family to all the nations.

Paul writes to the Ephesians, most of them Gentiles by birth, and asks them to remember what they once were: “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.” Then comes the great turning: “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.” The image comes from the Temple in Jerusalem, where a barrier kept Gentile visitors from the inner courts. In the Cross, Christ creates “in himself one new humanity in place of the two”, reconciling both to God in one body. And Paul draws the conclusion that every baptised Indian Christian can read as his own: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.” Our society still knows many dividing walls: of caste, of language, of wealth, of region and politics. Sadly, they have sometimes stood even inside our churches. The Ephesian letter says plainly that in the household of God those walls have already been broken down by the blood of Christ. It is our task not to rebuild them.

The Gospel lets us listen to Jesus praying on the night before he died. After praying for his disciples, he looks beyond them to us: “I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.” The unity Jesus asks for is not a mere agreement or a good organisation; it is a share in the communion of the Father and the Son. And it is missionary: “so that the world may believe.” Divided Christians make the Gospel hard to believe. We feel this pain in Kerala, where the descendants of the Christians of St Thomas now belong to several Churches. The Catholic Church prays and works for the full unity Christ willed, with respect and love for our brothers and sisters of the other Churches (Unitatis Redintegratio 1). The prayer ends with a desire that turns our minds to the Ascension: “Father, I desire that those also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory, which you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.” Where he goes on Thursday, he wants us to follow. Until then, the sign that we belong to him is the love that makes us one: “so that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
conn: How beautiful are the feet.
Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 for every preacher: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Romans 10:15).
A house of prayer for all peoples.
Isaiah 56:7 promises, “for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples”; Jesus recalls it in the Temple (Mark 11:17).
God shows no partiality.
In the house of Cornelius Peter says, “I truly understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34).
Repentance that leads to life.
The Church in Jerusalem praises God: “Then God has given even to the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life” (Acts 11:18).
The cornerstone.
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22); Christ is the cornerstone of the household of God (Ephesians 2:20).
One flock, one shepherd.
“I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold... So there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16).
One heart and soul.
The first community was “of one heart and soul” (Acts 4:32): the answer to Jesus' prayer begins in the Church at Jerusalem.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the sacrament of the unity for which Jesus prayed: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17). At the altar the dividing walls fall, and rich and poor, near and far, receive the same Lord.
Before Communion we exchange the peace. Christ is our peace; the sign of peace is a promise to live as members of one household.
outline: Opening
The threshold of the Ascension: a farewell and a sending.
Point 1 · How beautiful are the feet
The messenger of peace and the salvation of all the nations.
Point 2 · What God has made clean
Peter's vision and the open door for the Gentiles.
Point 3 · He is our peace
The dividing wall broken down, and the household of God.
Point 4 · That they may all be one
Jesus' prayer for us, and the pain of division.
Closing image
A Sunday Qurbana where a migrant worker, a farmer and a doctor kneel side by side at the same rail.
Take-home line
“That they may all be one... so that the world may believe.”
live: Break down one wall (Ephesians 2:14)
Speak kindly this week to someone your family or community keeps at a distance.
Pray for Christian unity (John 17:21)
Pray each day this week for the unity of the Churches, especially the Churches of the St Thomas tradition.
Carry the good news (Isaiah 52:7)
Share one word of faith or hope with someone who needs it.
Prepare for Thursday
Plan to take part in the Holy Qurbana of the Ascension on Thursday, a day of obligation.
fathers: St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)

Christ joins believers to himself and to one another through the mystical blessing of his own Body. Though many, we become one body in him by sharing the one Bread, and so his prayer that we may be one is fulfilled at the table of the Eucharist.
St Augustine (in substance)
The cornerstone joins two walls coming from different directions. One wall came from the circumcision, the other from the Gentiles; they met in Christ the corner, and there they became one house.
magis: Catechism 820
Christ gave unity to his Church from the beginning, and the Church must always pray and work to maintain, reinforce and perfect it.
Catechism 821
The desire to recover the unity of all Christians is a gift of Christ and a call of the Holy Spirit; it requires conversion of heart, common prayer and fraternal knowledge of one another.
Catechism 839
The relationship of the Church with the Jewish people: to them belong the sonship, the glory, the covenants and the promises; the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.
Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate 4
The Church remembers the spiritual bond that ties her to the stock of Abraham, and rejects every form of contempt for the Jewish people.
Second Vatican Council, Unitatis Redintegratio 1
Division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ, scandalises the world and damages the preaching of the Gospel.
saints: Today
Sixth Sunday of Resurrection. St Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria and defender of the faith of Nicaea, gives way to the Sunday this year. In the Latin calendar, the Sixth Sunday of Easter.
This week

3–8 May. Mon 3: Sts Philip and James, Apostles. Thu 6: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, a day of obligation. Fri 7: First Friday, and the first day of the waiting for the Holy Spirit with Mary. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May (verify locally).
2027-05-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, before your Passion you prayed to the Father that all who believe in you may be one. By your blood you have broken down the walls that divide us and made us members of one household. Make our feet beautiful with the good news of peace; open our hearts as you opened the heart of Peter; heal the divisions among Christians and in our society; and draw us after you to the glory where you are, until the world believes that the Father sent you. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-06.title: The Ascension of our Lord
2027-05-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Elijah is taken up to heaven
As they were watching, he was lifted up
One mediator between God and humankind
He withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven
2027-05-06.alt: Sixth Thursday of Resurrection: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, a Feast of Our Lord, an important feast and a day of obligation in the Syro-Malabar Church. Longer forms in the calendar: 2 Kings 2:1–15; Acts 1:1–14; 1 Timothy 1:18–2:15; Luke 24:36–53. St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May; in the Latin calendar today is a weekday of Easter there (verify locally). The Queen of Heaven is still prayed until Pentecost.
2027-05-06.verse: While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.
theo: Forty days after Easter the Church celebrates the Ascension of our Lord. The Acts of the Apostles tells us that after his suffering Jesus “presented himself alive to them by many convincing proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3), and then, from the Mount of Olives, he was taken up. Our Syro-Malabar Church keeps this day on the Thursday, as the ancient Church did, as a Feast of our Lord and a day of obligation; in the Syriac tradition it is called Sullaqa, the going up. (The Latin Church in India celebrates it this year on Sunday 9 May.) What do we celebrate? Not that Jesus has left us. The Creed says: “He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father.” The same Jesus who was born of the Virgin Mary, who died and rose in his body, now enters with that body, glorified and bearing the wounds, into the glory of God. For the first time a human nature, our nature, is at the right hand of the Father. That is why the Church can sing on this day with joy rather than sadness. Where the Head has gone, the members hope to follow (Catechism 661). And from there, Peter will say at Pentecost, “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear” (Acts 2:33). The Ascension is the hinge between Easter and Pentecost.

The calendar opens the feast with a story from the Old Testament that the first Christians read as a prophecy of this day: the taking up of Elijah. The old prophet knows that the Lord is about to take him, and three times he tells his disciple Elisha to stay behind, at Gilgal, at Bethel, at Jericho. Three times Elisha answers, “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” At the Jordan Elijah strikes the water with his mantle and they cross on dry ground. Then the master asks, “Tell me what I may do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha asks a great thing: “Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.” The answer is a condition: “if you see me as I am being taken from you, it will be granted you”. And then “a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah ascended in a whirlwind into heaven.” Elisha keeps watching and cries out, “Father, father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” Elisha saw, and so he received the spirit of his master; the mantle that fell from Elijah became his, and with it he struck the Jordan and it parted again. The disciples of Jesus are in Elisha's place. They watch their Master go up, and ten days later they will receive, not a double share of a prophet's spirit, but the Holy Spirit himself, the Spirit of the Son. Jesus had said it plainly: “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). The mantle of Christ is the Church's mission, and it has fallen on us.

In the Acts of the Apostles the disciples ask one last question: “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” Even after the Resurrection they are thinking of a kingdom like the kingdoms they knew. Jesus does not scold them; he redirects them: “It is not for you to know the times or periods that the Father has set by his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” The kingdom will come, but not by a calendar we can study; it will come through witnesses filled with the Spirit, moving outward from Jerusalem. One of those witnesses, Thomas, would carry the Gospel to the ends of the earth as Kerala then was. “When he had said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.” In Scripture the cloud is the sign of God's presence: the cloud that led Israel in the desert, the cloud that filled the Temple, the cloud of the Transfiguration. Jesus is not travelling through space to a distant place; he is entering the presence of God, where he is near to every place. And then two men in white robes ask the question that the Church hears every year on this feast: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” The Ascension does not give us permission to stand staring at the sky. It sends us back to Jerusalem, to prayer, to the Spirit and to the work of witness, until he comes again.

The Epistle shows us what Christ does now at the right hand of the Father. “First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for everyone, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and dignity.” Why should the Church pray for everyone, including rulers who may not know God? Because God “desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself a ransom for all”. Notice the words “himself human”. The one Mediator who has entered heaven is a man, our brother, who has not laid aside our nature. The Letter to the Hebrews says that “he entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and that “he always lives to make intercession” for those who approach God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When our Church prays in the Holy Qurbana for the Pope and the bishops, for rulers and for the whole world, for the sick and the departed, she prays with the ascended Christ and through him. Our prayers for the saints' intercession and for one another do not compete with his one mediation; they share in it, as members share in the life of the Head (Catechism 2634–2636).

Luke's Gospel ends with the same event told in a few unforgettable lines. Jesus opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: “Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” He promises the gift of the Father: “so stay here in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.” Then “he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.” The last image the apostles kept of Jesus on earth was of his raised, pierced hands, blessing them. Like a priest at the end of the Qurbana, he blesses and goes, and the blessing remains. And the disciples' response is surprising: “they worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually in the temple blessing God.” Joy, not sorrow; worship, not loss. Acts adds that in the upper room they “were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). From tomorrow the Church enters these days of waiting with the Blessed Virgin Mary; many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit, as Pope Leo XIII asked in 1897. Let us go up the mountain today with the apostles, receive his blessing, and come down with great joy to wait and pray for the Spirit.
conn: God has gone up with a shout.
“God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5): the Church sings this psalm on the Ascension.
Sit at my right hand.

“The Lord says to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1); “the Lord Jesus... was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).
One like a human being.
Daniel saw “one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven” and brought before the Ancient One (Daniel 7:13).
I go to prepare a place.
“If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also” (John 14:3).
I am ascending to my Father.
To Mary Magdalene: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17).
He gave gifts.
“When he ascended on high he made captivity itself a captive; he gave gifts to his people” (Ephesians 4:8).
The heavens opened.
Stephen, dying, sees “the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!” (Acts 7:56).
I am with you always.
Matthew's Gospel ends not with a departure but with a promise: “And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
Seek the things above.
“So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the ascended Lord is not far away. He who is seated at the right hand of the Father comes down upon our altar in his Body and Blood, and lifts us up with him. St Leo the Great said that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed into the sacraments.
Luke's Gospel ends with Jesus lifting up his hands to bless his disciples. Every Qurbana ends with a blessing given in his name: the hands of the ascended Christ are still raised over his people.
Before the anaphora the priest invites us to lift up our minds on high. On this feast we understand why: our Head is there, and in the Qurbana heaven and earth are joined.
outline: Opening
Forty days, the Mount of Olives, and a human nature at the right hand of the Father.
Point 1 · If you see me as I am being taken
Elijah's mantle and the double share of the Spirit.
Point 2 · Why do you stand looking up toward heaven?
The cloud, the promise of his return, and the call to witness.
Point 3 · One mediator, himself human
The ascended Christ intercedes for us; the Church prays for all.
Point 4 · Lifting up his hands, he blessed them
Great joy, the upper room, and the days of waiting with Mary.
Closing image
A family coming home from the Ascension Qurbana and gathering that evening before the picture of the Holy Spirit to begin the novena.
Take-home line
“While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.”
live: Keep the day holy
Take part in the Holy Qurbana today, a day of obligation, and make it a day of thanksgiving.
Begin the days of waiting (Acts 1:14)
Begin tomorrow a novena to the Holy Spirit, with your family, together with Mary.
Pray for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1)
Pray today by name for those in authority, in the nation, the state, the Church and your workplace.
Be a witness (Acts 1:8)
Tell one person this week what the risen and ascended Lord means to you.
Look up and go down
Spend a few minutes tonight under the open sky, thanking Christ for preparing a place for you, then do one concrete act of service.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Christ is now exalted above the heavens, yet he still suffers on earth in his members, saying, Saul, why do you persecute me? While he is in heaven he is also with us; and we, while on earth, are with him. He did not leave heaven when he came down to us, and he has not left us when he went up again.
St Leo the Great (in substance)

The Ascension of Christ is our own elevation; where the glory of the Head has gone, the hope of the body is called. What was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments, so that faith might be more excellent and firm.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Our nature, which had been driven out of paradise and was unworthy even of the earth, today ascends above the angels and the cherubim and is seated on the royal throne. The Lord has taken up the first fruits of our race and presented them to the Father.
magis: Catechism 659
The body of the risen Christ, after forty days, enters into the divine glory, symbolised by the cloud and by heaven, where he is seated at the right hand of God.
Catechism 661
The Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain, from where he will come again; we have the hope of following him there.
Catechism 662
Jesus Christ, the one priest of the new and eternal covenant, entered into heaven itself, where he permanently exercises his priesthood, for he always lives to make intercession for us.
Catechism 663–664
Being seated at the right hand of the Father signifies the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom, which will have no end.
Catechism 667
Jesus Christ, having entered the sanctuary of heaven once and for all, intercedes constantly for us as the mediator who assures us of the permanent outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 2634
Intercession is a prayer of petition which leads us to pray as Jesus did; he is the one intercessor with the Father on behalf of all.
saints: Today

THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, Sixth Thursday of Resurrection, a day of obligation. St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on Sunday 9 May (verify locally).
This week

Fri 7: First Friday, and the beginning of the days of waiting for the Holy Spirit with Mary (novena to the Holy Spirit, 7–15 May). Sat 8. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension. Pentecost: Sunday 16 May.
2027-05-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, today you ascended above the heavens and took our human nature to the right hand of the Father. As you blessed your apostles with raised hands, bless us also, and fill us with their great joy. You are the one mediator between God and humankind: intercede for us, for our families and for the whole world. Do not let us stand idly looking up, but send us back to pray and to bear witness. Prepare our hearts, with your Mother Mary, for the Spirit whom you have promised, and draw us, your members, to the place where you, our Head, have gone before us. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-09.title: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection (the Sunday after the Ascension)
2027-05-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Matthias is added to the eleven apostles
Every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord
Go into all the world and proclaim the good news
2027-05-09.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The Sunday after the Ascension (Thursday 6 May), and the third day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. Longer forms in the calendar: Philippians 1:27–2:11 and Mark 16:9–20. In the Latin Church in India the Ascension of the Lord is celebrated today, in place of the Seventh Sunday of Easter. Many dioceses also keep the World Day of Social Communications on this Sunday before Pentecost (verify locally).
2027-05-09.verse: Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And I said, “Here am I; send me!”
theo: This is the Sunday after the Ascension. Three days ago we watched the Lord taken up; next Sunday we will celebrate the coming of the Spirit. Today the Church stands in between, and the four readings tell one story: the Lord who reigns in glory sends people out. The Gospel of Mark ends with that double movement. The Risen Lord appears to the eleven “as they were sitting at the table”; he reproaches them for their unbelief, and then, astonishingly, he entrusts the whole world to these same slow-hearted men: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” Then “the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” And the last verse of the Gospel says: “they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that accompanied it.” The Lord is seated in heaven and working on earth at the same time. That is the meaning of the Ascension for the Church: he has not gone away from his work; he does it now through us. One of those eleven was Thomas, and the good news he carried reached our shores. Every Syro-Malabar Christian who hears this Gospel is the fruit of that sending.

The first reading shows us the throne from which the sending comes. “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lofty; and the hem of his robe filled the temple.” The seraphs cry to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.” We sing that hymn in every Holy Qurbana, joining the angels before the throne of the One who has ascended. Isaiah's first response is fear: “Woe is me! I am lost, for I am a man of unclean lips.” Then a seraph touches his lips with a live coal from the altar, and says, “your guilt has departed and your sin is blotted out.” Syriac Fathers such as St Ephrem saw in that coal, taken from the altar with tongs and placed on the lips, a figure of the Holy Qurbana, the fire of the Lord's Body given to us. Only after he is purified does Isaiah hear the question: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And he answers, “Here am I; send me!” The mission that follows is hard: the people will not listen, the land will be laid waste. Yet the chapter ends with hope: “The holy seed is its stump.” God never abandons his people; from the stump of Jesse the Messiah will come.

The Acts of the Apostles shows the Church obeying that sending in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. Just before today's reading we hear that the apostles “were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Then Peter stands up among about a hundred and twenty believers. The circle of the Twelve has been broken by the betrayal of Judas, and it must be restored before the Spirit comes. The one chosen must be a witness: “one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.” They propose two, Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias. They do not campaign; they pray: “Lord, you know everyone's heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen.” The lot falls on Matthias, “and he was added to the eleven apostles.” Here, in the presence of Mary, we see the apostolic Church taking care for its own continuity: the ministry of the apostles is handed on. Our bishops stand in that same line of witnesses, and the Synod of our Church still begins its elections with prayer to the Lord who knows every heart.

Paul's letter to the Philippians sings the whole mystery we are celebrating. “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness.” He went down, all the way to the Cross. “Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” The Ascension is that exaltation made visible: the One who emptied himself now sits at the right hand of God. But Paul did not write this hymn only to tell us about Christ; he wrote it to change the way the Philippians lived together. “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility regard others as better than yourselves.” The way up for the Church is the way Christ went: the way down, in humility and service. A parish quarrelling about positions, a family where everyone wants the first place, will not proclaim the Gospel well. A community that has the mind of Christ will be sent, like Isaiah and like the eleven, and the Lord will work with it.
conn: Holy, holy, holy.
Before the throne the living creatures sing without ceasing, “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God the Almighty, who was and is and is to come” (Revelation 4:8).
Isaiah's glory was Christ's.
John says of Isaiah's vision: “Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke about him” (John 12:41).
The stump of Jesse.
“A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1).
Mary in the upper room.
“All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus, as well as his brothers” (Acts 1:14).
Twelve thrones.
Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit “on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28): the number of the apostles is restored before Pentecost.
Every knee shall bow.
God swears in Isaiah: “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear” (Isaiah 45:23); Paul applies it to Jesus.
Seated at the right hand.
“The LORD says to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1).
The sending by Thomas.
Thomas, among the eleven who heard “Go into all the world”, is honoured by our Church as the apostle who brought the Gospel to India.
altar: In the Holy Qurbana we sing with the seraphs, “Holy, holy, holy”, before the throne of the Lord who has ascended. And like Isaiah we receive on our lips the live coal from the altar: the Body and Blood of Christ, which take away our guilt and make us ready to be sent.
At the end of the Qurbana we are sent out, as the eleven were sent. The Lord who is seated at the right hand of God goes with us and works with us through the week.
outline: Opening
Between the Ascension and Pentecost: the Lord in glory sends people out.
Point 1 · Holy, holy, holy
Isaiah's vision, the live coal, and “Here am I; send me!”
Point 2 · One must become a witness
Matthias, the hundred and twenty, and Mary in the upper room.
Point 3 · He emptied himself, therefore God exalted him
The hymn of Philippians and the humility of the Church.
Point 4 · Go into all the world
The commissioning, the Ascension, and the Lord who works with us.
Closing image
A small fishing boat at Kodungallur, where tradition says Thomas landed, and a Gospel that crossed the sea.
Take-home line
“Here am I; send me!”
live: Sing the Holy, holy, holy with attention (Isaiah 6:3)
At the Qurbana today, sing the angels' hymn slowly, knowing you stand before the throne of the Ascended Lord.
Say “send me” (Isaiah 6:8)
Offer the Lord one concrete service in your parish or neighbourhood this week, and tell your priest or a parish leader.
Pray for our bishops (Acts 1:24)
Pray daily this week for the bishops of the Syro-Malabar Synod, successors of the apostles, that the Lord who knows every heart may guide them.
Have the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:3)
In one quarrel or competition at home or at work, choose to give the first place to the other.
Share the good news (Mark 16:15)
Send a word of faith, a Gospel verse or an invitation to the Qurbana to one person who has drifted away; use the media well on this Sunday of social communications.
fathers: St Ephrem (in substance)

The seraph did not touch the coal with his fingers but took it with tongs; yet to us the Lord gives the fire into our own hands and onto our lips. The coal that touched Isaiah's lips forgave his sins; the Bread that is placed in our mouths, filled with fire and Spirit, makes us holy.
St Leo the Great (in substance)

What was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments. After the Ascension our faith grows stronger, because it no longer depends on sight: we believe in the One whom we do not see, seated at the right hand of the Father, and we meet him in the mysteries of the Church.
magis: Catechism 208
Before the glory of the thrice-holy God, Isaiah cries out, “Woe is me! I am lost.” Before the holy God man discovers his own insignificance; yet God who is holy can forgive and purify.
Catechism 659–664

The Lord's Body is taken up into heaven and he sits at the right hand of God: the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom. Being seated at the Father's right hand signifies that he shares the glory and honour of the divinity.
Catechism 861–862

The apostles took care to appoint successors, so that the mission entrusted to them might continue after their death; the bishops have by divine institution taken the place of the apostles as pastors of the Church.
Catechism 461 and 449

The Word became flesh, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant; the hymn of Philippians 2 confesses that God has given him the name above every name, and that every tongue shall confess Jesus Christ as Lord.
Catechism 849
The Church, sent by God to the nations, strives to preach the Gospel to all, obeying the missionary mandate of her founder.
saints: Today
Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension. In the Latin Church in India, the Ascension of the Lord. Third day of the novena to the Holy Spirit.
This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
Next Sunday
16 May: Pentecost, First Sunday of the Apostles; the Season of the Apostles begins.
2027-05-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you emptied yourself and became obedient unto death, and the Father has exalted you and seated you at his right hand. With the seraphs we cry, Holy, holy, holy. Touch our lips with the live coal of your altar, take away our guilt, and make us answer, Here am I; send me. Guide the successors of your apostles as you guided the choice of Matthias. Give us your mind, humble and loving, so that our communities may proclaim you. Work with us, Lord, wherever you send us, until every tongue confesses that you are Lord, to the glory of the Father. With Mary your Mother we pray: send us your Holy Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-16.title: First Sunday of the Apostles · The Feast of Pentecost
2027-05-16.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A priestly kingdom and a holy nation
The Holy Spirit comes down on the apostles
Varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit
The Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth
2027-05-16.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), the seven weeks that begin at Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari; from Pentecost “The Angel of the Lord” (the Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Pentecost is a Feast of Our Lord, and the Season of the Apostles (Šleehe) begins today. The calendar gives longer forms: Exodus 19:1–9 with 20:13–21; Acts 2:1–21; 1 Corinthians 12:1–27; John 14:15–16, 25–26; 15:26–16:15. In the Latin calendar Pentecost Sunday closes the Easter season today. St Simon Stock (16 May) gives way to the feast (verify locally).
2027-05-16.verse: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
theo: Fifty days ago we sang the Resurrection; today the fifty days reach their goal. “When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.” Pentecost was already a great feast for the Jewish people, the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival kept fifty days after Passover, and in later Jewish tradition it was also linked with the giving of the Law on Sinai. That is why our Church opens the feast with Exodus 19. “On the third new moon after the Israelites had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that very day, they came into the wilderness of Sinai.” God speaks to Moses from the mountain: “You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.” Then the promise: “you shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.” God comes in a dense cloud, and a few verses later the mountain is wrapped in smoke “because the LORD had descended upon it in fire” (Exodus 19:18). At Sinai, fire on the mountain gave Israel the Law on tablets of stone; in the upper room, fire on each head writes the new law of love on human hearts, as the prophet had promised: “I will put my spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27). The people at Sinai answered, “Everything that the LORD has spoken we will do”; at Pentecost the Spirit gives the power to do it. Peter would later write to the baptised the very words of Sinai: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people” (1 Peter 2:9).

Luke describes the event with signs that every reader of the Scriptures would recognise. “Suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.” Wind and breath are one word in Hebrew and in our Syriac tradition: the breath God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the wind Ezekiel summoned over the dry bones, the breath of the Risen Lord who said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). “Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.” The Spirit does not come as a general mood over a crowd; a tongue rests on each one. And the first thing the Spirit does is make them speak. The Church is born speaking, born on mission. The disciples who had hidden behind locked doors now go out into the street. Mary is among them; the Spirit who overshadowed her at Nazareth to form the body of Christ now comes down to form his Body, the Church.

The crowd that gathers is made of “devout Jews from every nation under heaven living in Jerusalem”, and each one hears the apostles “speaking in the native language of each.” Then Luke lists the nations, and we Syro-Malabar Christians should listen closely: “Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia”. These are the lands of the East where the Gospel soon took root, the lands of the Church of the East, whose faith, liturgy and Syriac language came to the Thomas Christians of Malabar. At Pentecost our own spiritual ancestors were, in a sense, already standing in the crowd. At Babel human pride had confused the languages and scattered the peoples (Genesis 11:9); at Pentecost the Spirit does not abolish the languages but makes the one Gospel heard in each of them. That is why the Church can pray in Syriac and Malayalam, in Latin and Tamil, in English and Hindi, and still be one. The reaction is mixed: “All were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, ‘What does this mean?’ But others sneered and said, ‘They are filled with new wine.’” The Spirit's work always provokes both wonder and mockery. Joel had promised, and Peter will soon proclaim, that God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh (Acts 2:16–17). It has happened.

Paul tells the Corinthians how to recognise the Spirit. Not by spectacle, but by a confession: “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except by the Holy Spirit.” Every time a child in our homes lisps the name of Jesus, every time a dying person whispers, Eeshoye, the Spirit is at work. Then Paul describes the Church as a body with many gifts: “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who activates all of them in everyone.” Notice the Holy Trinity in those three lines: Spirit, Lord, God. The gifts differ: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, prophecy, discernment, tongues. But the purpose is one: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” No gift is for showing off, and no one is without a gift. The catechist who teaches on Sunday morning, the choir member, the parent who prays with the children, the youth who visits the sick, the elderly woman who prays the rosary for the parish: all of these “are activated by one and the same Spirit, who allots to each one individually just as the Spirit chooses.” We received the seal of this Spirit in our Thailabhishekam, the anointing with holy Myron given in our Church together with Baptism.

In the Gospel Jesus prepares his disciples for this day. They are sad that he is leaving, and he says something astonishing: “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” The Ascension was not a loss; it opened the way for the gift. The Spirit will “prove the world wrong about sin and righteousness and judgment”: he shows the world its sin of unbelief, reveals the righteousness of Christ who returns to the Father, and announces that “the ruler of this world has been condemned.” And for the disciples: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth”. He does not invent a new Gospel: “he will take what is mine and declare it to you. All that the Father has is mine.” Here, on the threshold of next Sunday's feast of the Holy Trinity, we glimpse the life of God: the Father who gives all to the Son, the Son who sends the Spirit, the Spirit who glorifies the Son. Today the Season of the Apostles begins, the seven weeks in which our Church contemplates how the Spirit sent the apostles to the ends of the earth, and how one of them, Mar Thoma, came to our shores. The Spirit who came down in the upper room is the same Spirit who keeps the faith alive in Kerala homes and parishes. Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.
conn: Babel undone.
At Babel “the LORD confused the language of all the earth; and from there the LORD scattered them abroad” (Genesis 11:9); at Pentecost the scattered hear one Gospel in their own languages (Acts 2:6).
Fire on the mountain.
Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke “because the LORD had descended upon it in fire” (Exodus 19:18); at Pentecost tongues as of fire rest on each disciple (Acts 2:3).
The breath of life.
God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); the Risen Lord “breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22).
Clothed with power.
“So stay here in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49); “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8).
Would that all were prophets.
Moses longed: “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29); Joel promised it (Joel 2:28).
The Spirit on the Messiah.

“The spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2); the Spirit who rested on Christ is given to his Body.
Love poured out.
“God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).
altar: In every Holy Qurbana the priest calls down the Holy Spirit upon the bread and wine in the Epiclesis, and the Spirit who came at Pentecost makes them the Body and Blood of Christ. Pentecost happens again on our altar.
The same Spirit is asked to come upon us, that we who receive the one Body may become one body, each with our gift, for the common good.
outline: Opening
Fifty days, and the harvest feast of Israel.
Point 1 · A priestly kingdom and a holy nation
Sinai, the cloud, the fire and the law written on hearts.
Point 2 · A tongue rested on each
Wind, fire and the Church born speaking; Mary in the upper room.
Point 3 · Each heard in their own language
Parthians, Medes, Mesopotamia: our own ancestors in faith, and Babel undone.
Point 4 · Varieties of gifts, the same Spirit
Jesus is Lord, and gifts for the common good.
Closing image
The Spirit of truth guiding the Church, and Mar Thoma landing on our shore.
Take-home line
“Come, Holy Spirit.”
live: Say “Jesus is Lord” (1 Corinthians 12:3)
Begin and end each day this week by saying slowly: Jesus is Lord, and ask the Spirit to make it true in you.
Name your gift (1 Corinthians 12:7)
Ask yourself what gift the Spirit has given you, and offer it this month to your parish for the common good.
Speak the Gospel in another's language (Acts 2:6)
Explain your faith this week to someone in words they understand: a child, a colleague, a friend of another faith, with respect.
Pray the Angelus again (from today)
From today pray “The Angel of the Lord” at morning, noon and evening, as our Church does in the Season of the Apostles.
fathers: St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

As dry flour cannot become one loaf without water, so we who are many could not become one in Christ without the water that comes from heaven. Our bodies received unity through the washing of baptism, and our souls through the Spirit, the dew of God poured out at Pentecost.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

The rain that comes down from heaven is one and the same, yet it becomes white in the lily, red in the rose, purple in the violet. So the Holy Spirit, one and undivided, gives to each as he wills: to one wisdom, to another prophecy, to another the power to drive out demons, and the Spirit himself is not changed.
magis: Catechism 732
On that day the Holy Trinity is fully revealed; the Kingdom announced by Christ is open to those who believe in him, and the Church is manifested to the world.
Catechism 767

When the work the Father gave the Son was accomplished, the Holy Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost to sanctify the Church continually; then the Church was openly displayed to the crowds and the spread of the Gospel began.
Catechism 729

Only when the hour has arrived for his glorification does Jesus promise the coming of the Holy Spirit; the Spirit will be with the disciples for ever, teaching them and guiding them into all the truth.
Catechism 797
What the soul is to the human body, the Holy Spirit is to the Body of Christ, which is the Church (St Augustine).
Catechism 799–800

Charisms, extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit that directly or indirectly benefit the Church; they are to be accepted with gratitude, and charity is the true measure of them.
saints: Today

First Sunday of the Apostles, the Feast of Pentecost, a Feast of Our Lord; the Season of the Apostles begins. In the Latin calendar Pentecost Sunday, which closes the Easter season. St Simon Stock gives way to the feast.
Next week

17–23 May: first week of the Apostles. Mon 17: Mary, Mother of the Church (listed in the First Set without proper readings; in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Thu 20: anniversary of the inauguration of the first Syro-Malabar Bishops' Synod (1993). Fri 21: the Friday of Gold, the first Friday of the Apostles. Sun 23: Second Sunday of the Apostles, the Feast of the Holy Trinity.
2027-05-16.prayer: Father, on this holy day you fulfilled the promise of your Son and sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles gathered with Mary, the Mother of Jesus. Pour out the same Spirit on your Church spread throughout the world, on our Syro-Malabar Church, heir of Mar Thoma, and on our families. As at Sinai you made a holy nation, make us a priestly people who live by the law of love written on our hearts. Let the Spirit of truth guide us into all the truth, give each of us our gift for the common good, and loosen our tongues to proclaim in every language that Jesus is Lord. Glory to you, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-23.title: Second Sunday of the Apostles · Feast of the Most Holy Trinity
2027-05-23.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I am your God, who teaches and leads you
God's love poured out through the Holy Spirit
The Spirit of truth will guide you
2027-05-23.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives two sets of readings for this day. The readings of the feast of the Holy Trinity are given above, and this page is built on them. Readings of the Second Sunday of the Apostles: Joel 2:18–26; Acts 4:8–22; 1 Corinthians 6:1–11; Luke 7:36–50 (longer forms in the calendar: Joel 2:15–26; Acts 4:5–22; 1 Corinthians 5:6–6:11; Luke 7:31–50). Verify locally which set your parish reads. St Rita, listed for 23 May in the First Set, gives way to the feast.
2027-05-23.verse: And hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
theo: One week after Pentecost the Church lifts her eyes from all that God has done to who God is. In the Season of the Apostles we have recalled the coming of the Spirit, the first healing in the Name of Jesus, the Church as one Body. Today we adore the source of it all: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Catechism calls the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity “the central mystery of Christian faith and life”, the mystery of God in himself and the light that shines on every other mystery (CCC 234). We did not invent it, and no philosopher discovered it. God revealed it by acting: the Father sent the Son, and the Father and the Son sent the Spirit. This is why our faith begins and ends in the Name. We were baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19); we sign ourselves with the Cross in that Name; every Holy Qurbana begins and ends with the glory of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Church of the East has always loved to sing it. The Trinity is not a puzzle for scholars. It is the family into which we have been born again.

The readings for the feast begin under the oaks of Mamre. “The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day. He looked up and saw three men standing near him.” Abraham runs to meet them, bows to the ground, and calls them “My lord”, in the singular. He washes their feet, Sarah bakes cakes from the finest flour, a tender calf is prepared, “and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.” The text does not say that Abraham saw the Trinity; the Old Testament does not yet reveal the three Persons. But the Fathers of the Church, reading this page in the light of Christ, saw in the three visitors who speak as one Lord a hint of the mystery to come, and the Christian East has painted it again and again as the icon of the Hospitality of Abraham. Two lessons stay with us. God comes as a guest, and he is welcomed by hospitality: “some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). And the God who is three Persons in one communion of love is himself, in a sense, eternal welcome: the Father gives everything to the Son, the Son returns everything to the Father, and, as St Augustine taught, the Spirit is the love between them.

Isaiah gives us the voice of the one God who is “the first” and “the last”. “Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last.” His hand laid the foundation of the earth and spread out the heavens. And then a striking line: “And now the Lord GOD has sent me and his spirit.” The Fathers heard in it the Son speaking, sent by the Father with the Spirit. Whether or not the prophet saw so far, the Church reads this oracle today because it shows how God has always revealed himself: as the One who calls, who sends and who teaches. The reading ends with a tender promise: “I am the LORD your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.” The doctrine of the Trinity is not cold. It tells us that the God who made the heavens wants to walk with us on the road.

Paul, writing to Rome, shows the Trinity at work in the life of every believer. “Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand.” Peace with the Father, access through the Son. And then the third Person: “hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.” Notice that this happens in the middle of suffering: “we also boast in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope.” The Trinity does not float above our troubles. The Father reconciles us, the Son opens the door, and the Spirit pours love into hearts that are hurting. The Catechism uses this very verse to say that God is love, and love is his first gift, containing all the others (CCC 733).

In the Gospel Jesus, on the night before he died, tells the apostles: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” And he describes the life of God in three short sentences: the Spirit “will glorify me, because he will take what is mine and declare it to you. All that the Father has is mine.” Everything the Father has, he gives to the Son; everything of the Son, the Spirit makes known to us. The Church professes one God in three Persons, really distinct, yet one in nature, each wholly God (CCC 253–255). The Sunday readings, also set for today, show the same Trinity in our salvation: Paul tells the Corinthians, “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11); Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says that “there is no other name under heaven” (Acts 4:12); and the woman at Simon's table weeps at the feet of Jesus and hears, “Your sins are forgiven.” The Trinity is not far away. We are invited into it, and Jesus promises: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them” (John 14:23). The goal of our whole life is to enter the perfect unity of the Blessed Trinity (CCC 260).
conn: The God of three visitors.
Hebrews 13:2: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.”
The first and the last.
The Risen Christ takes the title of Isaiah 48:12: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 22:13).
In the one Name.
“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).
The blessing of the Three.
Paul ends a letter with the blessing used in our liturgies: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:13).
The Jordan.
At the baptism of Jesus the Father's voice is heard and the Spirit descends like a dove (Luke 3:21–22): the first clear revealing of the Three.
The Spirit of truth.
Jesus promised “the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father” who “will testify on my behalf” (John 15:26).
We will make our home.
“We will come to them and make our home with them” (John 14:23): the Trinity dwelling in the believer.
altar: Every Holy Qurbana is offered to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit: the great prayer of our Anaphora is the Church entering the life of the Trinity.
At the epiclesis the Church asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon the offerings; the Spirit who takes what is the Son's and gives it to us gives us the Body and Blood of Christ.
outline: Opening
A child making the sign of the Cross for the first time, and the whole faith in one gesture.
Point 1 · Three men at the oaks of Mamre
God the guest, welcomed by hospitality.
Point 2 · I am the first and I am the last
The God who calls, sends and teaches.
Point 3 · God's love poured into our hearts
The Father, the Son and the Spirit at work in our suffering and hope.
Point 4 · All that the Father has is mine
The Spirit of truth and the inner life of God.
Closing image
A family in Changanacherry praying the evening prayer together and ending, ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’
Take-home line
“God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.”
live: Make the sign of the Cross slowly
Each time today, make it with attention: you are naming the God into whose life you were baptized.
Welcome a guest (Genesis 18:2)
Invite someone lonely to your home this week and serve them as Abraham served the three visitors.
Offer a suffering (Romans 5:3)
Name one present trouble and pray: Father, through Jesus, by your Spirit, make this produce hope.
Pray the Glory Be
Pray ‘Glory to the Father…’ at the start and end of every task today, as the Church does at every hour.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

Look at the sun: the sun itself, its light and its warmth are distinct, yet they are not three suns but one. So the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three, yet one God; the light comes from the sun and is not separated from it, and the warmth comes from both.
St Augustine (in substance)

If you see love, you see the Trinity: there is the one who loves, the one who is loved, and the love itself. In God the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Father, and the Holy Spirit is the love by which they love each other.
magis: Catechism 234
The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is the central mystery of Christian faith and life; it is the mystery of God in himself and the source of all the other mysteries of faith.
Catechism 253–255
The Trinity is One: one God in three Persons; the divine Persons are really distinct from one another; they are relative to one another.
Catechism 244
The eternal origin of the Holy Spirit is revealed in his mission in time: the Spirit is sent by the Father in the name of the Son, and by the Son from the Father.
Catechism 733
God is love, and love is his first gift, containing all others: God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5).
Catechism 260
The ultimate end of the whole divine economy is the entry of God's creatures into the perfect unity of the Blessed Trinity.
saints: Today
Second Sunday of the Apostles, the feast of the Most Holy Trinity. In the Latin calendar, also the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity. St Rita (listed for 23 May in the First Set) gives way.
This week

23–29 May: second week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 23: the Most Holy Trinity. Tue 25: in the Latin calendar, St Bede the Venerable, St Gregory VII and St Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, kept by our Church on the Thursday (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Then Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles; Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-23.prayer: Holy Father, almighty God, you sent your only Son, the Word of truth, and your Holy Spirit, the giver of life, to make known to us the wonderful mystery of your being. We adore you, one God in three Persons, the first and the last, who teaches us and leads us on the way. As Abraham welcomed you under the oaks of Mamre, may we welcome you in every guest and stranger. Pour your love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, that our sufferings may become hope that does not disappoint. Lord Jesus, all that the Father has is yours; let your Spirit guide us into all the truth and make our hearts your home. To you, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, be glory, honour and thanksgiving, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.

2027-05-30.title: Third Sunday of the Apostles
2027-05-30.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You have stayed long enough at this mountain
A people who went astray from God
2027-05-30.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 1:3–17 and Luke 10:23–42 (with the visit to Martha and Mary). In India the Latin Church keeps the solemnity of Corpus Christi today; the Syro-Malabar Church kept the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ on Thursday 27 May.
2027-05-30.verse: He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
theo: Two weeks after Pentecost the Season of the Apostles shows us the Church on the move. The first reading is the beginning of Moses' great farewell speech on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the promised land. He recalls the word God spoke at Mount Horeb, forty years earlier: “You have stayed long enough at this mountain. Resume your journey, and go into the hill country of the Amorites.” Then the promise: “See, I have set the land before you; go in and take possession of the land that I swore to your ancestors, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Horeb, or Sinai, was the mountain of the covenant, the place where God had spoken. It would have been easy to stay there for ever. But the covenant was given for a journey. So it is with Pentecost. The apostles did not stay in the Upper Room; the Spirit sent them out to Samaria, to Antioch, to Rome, and, as our tradition holds, to the coasts of India with Mar Thoma. Every parish, every prayer group and every family is tempted to settle down on its own mountain of good experiences. The Lord says to us too: you have stayed long enough; resume your journey. The longer reading adds that Moses could not carry the people alone and appointed wise leaders, telling the judges: “hear out the small and the great alike; you shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s.” The Church on the move shares her burdens and is just to the small.

Isaiah opens his book with a lawsuit in which heaven and earth are the witnesses: “Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth; for the Lord has spoken: I reared children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib; but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.” The image is homely and painful. A farm animal knows the hand that feeds it and finds its way back to its own manger, but God's own children have forgotten him. The Fathers loved to see in this verse the ox and the donkey at the manger of Bethlehem, where the Lord of Israel lay in a feeding trough, recognised by animals and by shepherds. Isaiah describes a land wounded from head to foot, “bruises and sores and bleeding wounds; they have not been drained, or bound up, or softened with oil.” Remember those words when we come to the Gospel. And yet even here there is hope: “If the Lord of hosts had not left us a few survivors, we would have been like Sodom.” God always keeps a remnant, and through the remnant he begins again.

Paul answers questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage. Some among them, it seems, were saying, “It is well for a man not to touch a woman,” as though the married love of husband and wife were somehow unholy. Paul disagrees. Husband and wife belong to each other: “The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.” What is striking, in a world where wives were often treated as the property of their husbands, is that Paul speaks of perfect mutuality: neither has authority over his or her own body; each belongs to the other. Married couples may abstain for a time by agreement in order to give themselves to prayer, and then come together again. Then he adds: “I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has a particular gift from God, one having one kind and another a different kind.” Marriage is a gift; consecrated celibacy is a gift. Neither is to be despised, and each is a true path to holiness. Our Syro-Malabar Church, which crowns the bride and groom in the sacrament of Marriage and whose families have given so many priests and religious sisters to the world, knows both gifts. Today let us pray for married couples, especially those going through difficulties, and for all who have given their bodies and lives to God in priesthood and religious life.

The Gospel is one of the best-loved stories Jesus ever told. A lawyer asks, “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” He knows the answer himself: love God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and your neighbour as yourself. But “wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, ‘And who is my neighbor?’” He wants a boundary: who counts, and who does not? Jesus answers with a story. A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is stripped, beaten and left half dead. A priest passes by on the other side; so does a Levite. We are not told why, and we should not mock them; perhaps they feared ritual impurity, perhaps robbers. Jesus, a Jew speaking to a Jew, then names the one person his hearers least expected to be the hero: “But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity.” The Samaritan does all that Isaiah said no one had done for wounded Israel: he binds the wounds and pours in oil and wine. He takes him to an inn, pays, and promises to come back. Then Jesus turns the lawyer's question around: not, who is my neighbour, but “Which of these three, do you think, was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?” The lawyer cannot bring himself to say “the Samaritan”; he says, “The one who showed him mercy.” “Go and do likewise.” The Fathers saw in the Samaritan Christ himself, who came down to our wounded humanity, poured in the oil and wine of the sacraments, brought us to the inn of the Church and promised to return. Those who have been healed by such a Samaritan cannot pass by on the other side: not by the accident victim on the national highway, nor by the migrant worker far from home, nor by the neighbour of another caste or another religion.
conn: You have stayed long enough.

After the Resurrection Jesus says, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15); the Spirit sends the apostles from Jerusalem “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).
The ox and the donkey.
Isaiah 1:3 lies behind the ox and the donkey of the Christmas crib: Mary “laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn” (Luke 2:7).
Wounds not bound up.
Isaiah's wounded Israel (Isaiah 1:6) is healed by the Samaritan who “bandaged his wounds, having poured oil and wine on them” (Luke 10:34).
Come now, let us argue it out.
Later in the same chapter: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be like snow” (Isaiah 1:18).
Two in one flesh.
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24); “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church” (Ephesians 5:25).
Love your neighbour.
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the Lord” (Leviticus 19:18), quoted by the lawyer in Luke 10:27.
The least of these.
“Just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).
altar: The Good Samaritan pours oil and wine on the wounds: the Church has always seen in them the sacraments, the holy oils of Baptism, Confirmation and the Anointing of the Sick, and the wine that becomes the Blood of Christ in the Holy Qurbana. At this altar the true Samaritan binds our wounds.
He paid two denarii and promised to return. Until he comes again, the Church is his inn, and every Qurbana is the place where he cares for us and sends us out to care for others.
outline: Opening
From Horeb to the promised land, from the Upper Room to the nations: the Church on the move.
Point 1 · You have stayed long enough at this mountain
The covenant is given for a journey.
Point 2 · The ox knows its owner
A people who forgot God, and the remnant he keeps.
Point 3 · Each has a particular gift from God
Married love and consecrated celibacy as gifts.
Point 4 · Go and do likewise
Not who is my neighbour, but whose neighbour I become.
Closing image
A man lying by the national highway at night, and the one car that stops.
Take-home line
“Go and do likewise.”
live: Resume your journey (Deuteronomy 1:7)
Take one step out of your comfortable circle this week: visit a family in the parish you do not know, or join a mission activity.
Know your owner (Isaiah 1:3)
Begin and end each day this week with a short prayer at the family altar, so that the house knows to whom it belongs.
Honour the gift (1 Corinthians 7:7)
Married couples: pray together for five minutes each night this week. All: pray for a priest or religious sister you know.
Be a neighbour (Luke 10:36–37)
Do one concrete act of mercy this week for someone outside your own group, caste, religion or language.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The man who went down from Jerusalem is Adam, the human race; the robbers are the powers that strip us of grace and wound us. The Samaritan, whose name means guardian, is the Lord himself, who came near to us, bound our wounds, poured in the oil of hope and the wine of fervent spirit, and brought us to the inn, which is the Church.
Origen (in substance)

The Samaritan carries the wounded man on his own beast: Christ bears our sins in his own body. He promises to return and pay whatever more is spent: so he will reward at his coming those who care for the wounded in the inn of the Church.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Make your house a church. Let husband and wife teach each other and their children the things of God, pray together and read the Scriptures together, and their marriage will be a small Church.
magis: Catechism 1822
Charity is the theological virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbour as ourselves for the love of God.
Catechism 2447
The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily necessities.
Catechism 1643
Conjugal love involves a totality in which all the elements of the person enter; it aims at a deeply personal unity that leads to forming one heart and soul.
Catechism 1620

Both the sacrament of Matrimony and virginity for the Kingdom of God come from the Lord himself; esteem of virginity and the Christian understanding of marriage are inseparable and reinforce each other.
Pope Francis, Fratelli Tutti 67 and 81

The parable of the Good Samaritan shows how a community can be rebuilt by men and women who make the fragility of others their own; we are called to become neighbours to others, to cross every boundary.
saints: Today
Third Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar in India, the solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ (Corpus Christi), replacing the Ninth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Next days
Mon 31 May: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, closing the month of Mary. Fri 4 June: the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles).
2027-05-30.prayer: Lord God, you led your people from the mountain of the covenant toward the land you promised, and at Pentecost you sent your apostles to the ends of the earth. Do not let us settle on our own mountain, but send us out. Forgive us when we have forgotten you, though the ox knows its owner. Bless husbands and wives with faithful love, and those you have called to give themselves wholly to you with joy in their gift. Lord Jesus, true Samaritan, you came near to our wounds and poured in oil and wine: make us neighbours to everyone we meet, until you come again. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-05-01.title: Fifth Saturday of Resurrection · St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class
2027-05-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread
Send wisdom to labour at my side
Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus
Is not this the carpenter's son?
2027-05-01.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The First Set calendar lists St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class, on 1 May with the readings above (verify locally whether your parish keeps the feast readings). Weekday readings of the Fifth Saturday of Resurrection: Hebrews 7:11–17; John 15:26–16:4. In the Latin calendar St Joseph the Worker is an optional memorial, placed on 1 May by Pope Pius XII in 1955. Today is also May Day, Labour Day, and the first day of the month that our families dedicate to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-01.verse: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
theo: On the first day of May, when many nations honour working men and women, the Church turns to a working man of Nazareth. In 1955 Pope Pius XII placed a feast of St Joseph the Worker on this day, so that the workers of the world would have a patron and a model, and so that no one would think that the Church looks on labour from a distance. Our Syro-Malabar families know Joseph well. We call him Yauseppithavu, Father Joseph; we keep March as his month and Wednesday as his day; countless churches in Kerala bear his name, and many a family begins a new house or a new business with a prayer to him. Today's Gospel gives him the only title the people of Nazareth ever gave him: the carpenter. The word used in Matthew's Greek, tekton, means a craftsman, a builder who worked with wood and perhaps with stone, making ploughs and yokes, doors and roof beams for the village. Mark's Gospel gives the same title to Jesus himself: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mark 6:3). For about thirty years the Son of God lived in that workshop, learned the trade from Joseph, and earned his bread as the people around him did. The Church sees in this hidden life a great teaching: the greater part of the Saviour's life on earth was spent in ordinary work (Catechism 531–533).

The first reading takes us back to the beginning, to the words spoken to Adam after the first sin: “cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life”, and “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Then the man is sent out of the garden “to till the ground from which he was taken.” It would be easy to conclude that work itself is a punishment.
