Scripture says otherwise. Before there was any sin, “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work belonged to God's first plan for us; it is a share in his own care for creation. What sin brought was the thorns and thistles, the toil that wears us out, the sweat, the frustration, the work that seems never to bear fruit. The good news of Nazareth is that the Son of God entered into exactly this toil. The Second Vatican Council says that he worked with human hands and thought with a human mind (Gaudium et Spes 22). In the workshop of Joseph, sweat itself was taken up into the work of redemption. The farmer in Kuttanad, the woman at the tea estate in Munnar, the young nurse on a night shift in a hospital far from home: their sweat is not wasted when it is joined to his.

The second reading is the prayer of a king who knows that power and cleverness are not enough. Solomon asks God: “Send her forth from the holy heavens, and from the throne of your glory send her, that she may labor at my side, and that I may learn what is pleasing to you.” He admits frankly, “For the reasoning of mortals is worthless, and our designs are likely to fail”, and asks, “Who has learned your counsel, unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit from on high?” Joseph was such a man of wisdom, though he never sat on a throne. The Gospels do not record a single word from him; they record his obedience. Four times God spoke to him in a dream, and each time he rose and did what he was told: he took Mary as his wife, he fled with the child to Egypt, he returned, he settled in Nazareth (Matthew 1:20–24; 2:13–23). His wisdom was not a theory; it laboured at his side. In these last days before the Ascension and Pentecost, Solomon's prayer is the prayer of the whole Church: send your holy spirit from on high. Colossians tells us what such wisdom looks like in a household: “Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony”, and, “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.” That one verse could be written over the door of the house at Nazareth, and over the door of every Christian home and workplace.

In the Gospel Jesus comes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up are astounded: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?” Familiarity blinds them; “they took offense at him.” Jesus answers, “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house”, and Matthew adds a sad line: “he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.” Without knowing it, the villagers paid Joseph his greatest honour: the One who stood before them had been known for years simply as his son. The weekday readings of this Fifth Saturday complete the picture. Hebrews says that Jesus, born of the tribe of Judah and not of the priestly tribe, is a priest “through the power of an indestructible life”; the carpenter's son is the eternal high priest who offers himself for us. And in John Jesus promises, “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, he will testify on my behalf.” On this May Day we also remember the Church's long teaching on the dignity of work, from Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891) to St John Paul II's Laborem Exercens (1981), which says that work is for the human person, and not the person for work. We pray for those who have no work, for those who are paid unjustly, for the many workers from other states who build our houses in Kerala far from their families, and for our own sons and daughters who labour in the Gulf and across the world. St Joseph, patron of workers, pray for them all.
conn: To till it and keep it.
Before any sin, “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15): work is part of God's first plan.
The carpenter.
Mark gives the title to Jesus himself: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mark 6:3).
Paul at his trade.
Paul worked with his hands as a tentmaker at Corinth (Acts 18:3) and wrote: “Anyone unwilling to work should not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
Rest for the weary.
Jesus calls all who toil: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
Wages that cry out.
“Listen! The wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out” (James 5:4).
A priest forever.
Hebrews 7:17 quotes Psalm 110:4: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”
altar: At the offertory of the Holy Qurbana the priest places on the altar bread and wine, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands”, as the Latin liturgy says. In them we offer our own week of labour, and the Lord who worked at Joseph's bench takes it up into his sacrifice.
The hands that made ploughs in Nazareth were nailed to the Cross and now bless us from the altar. Every Qurbana makes holy the work we bring to it.
outline: Opening
May Day and the carpenter of Nazareth.
Point 1 · By the sweat of your face
Work in God's first plan, toil after the fall, and toil redeemed.
Point 2 · Wisdom that labours at my side
Solomon's prayer and Joseph's silent obedience.
Point 3 · Is not this the carpenter's son?
The hidden years, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Closing image
A father in Kerala closing his workshop at dusk and making the sign of the Cross before he goes home.
Take-home line
“Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
live: Offer your work (Colossians 3:17)
Begin your work today with a short prayer: Lord Jesus, I do this in your name.
Pay what is just (James 5:4)
If anyone works for you, at home or in business, make sure their wage is fair and paid on time.
Pray for those who labour far away
Pray today for one person you know who works far from home, in another state or abroad, and send them a message.
A May devotion
Begin the Marian month today with a decade of the Rosary at home, remembering the Holy Family at Nazareth.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Speaking of Paul, who sewed tents with his own hands, he says: let no one be ashamed of manual work. The apostle who preached to the nations was not ashamed to sit at the workbench. It is idleness that is disgraceful, not labour; work is a teacher of virtue.
St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

In his hymns on the Nativity he imagines Joseph with the child: Joseph held the Son as a little one and served him as God; he rejoiced in him as the Good One and stood in awe before him as the Just One.
magis: Catechism 531
During the greater part of his life Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of human beings: a daily life spent without evident greatness, a life of manual labour.
Catechism 2427

Human work comes from persons created in God's image; by enduring the hardship of work in union with Jesus, the carpenter of Nazareth and the one crucified on Calvary, we collaborate in a certain way with the Son of God in his work of redemption.
Catechism 2434
A just wage is the legitimate fruit of work; to refuse or withhold it can be a grave injustice.
St John Paul II, Laborem Exercens 6 (1981)
Work is for the human person, and not the person for work; the dignity of work comes from the one who works.
Pope Francis, Patris Corde (2020)
Joseph is a working father: from him Jesus learned the value, the dignity and the joy of eating bread that is the fruit of one's own labour.
saints: Today

St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class, in the First Set calendar; in the Latin calendar St Joseph the Worker (optional memorial). May Day. The month of May, dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, begins.
This week

1–6 May: the last days of the Resurrection season before the Ascension, in the month of May that our families dedicate to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Sat 1: St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class (May Day). Sun 2: Sixth Sunday of Resurrection; St Athanasius (2 May) gives way to the Sunday. Mon 3: Sts Philip and James, Apostles. Thu 6: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, an important feast and a day of obligation; St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May (verify locally).
2027-05-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you lived for many years as the carpenter's son at Nazareth and worked with human hands. Through the prayers of St Joseph, patron of workers, make holy the labour of our hands and minds. Give work to those who have none, justice to those who are paid unfairly, rest to the weary, and strength to all who toil far from home. Teach us to do everything in your name, giving thanks to the Father through you, and send us from on high the Spirit of wisdom, whom you have promised. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-03.title: Sixth Monday of Resurrection · Sts Philip and James, Apostles
2027-05-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously
The righteous will stand with great confidence
Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel
I am the way, and the truth, and the life
2027-05-03.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The First Set calendar keeps Sts Philip and James, Apostles, on 3 May with the readings above; the calendar gives the longer Gospel John 14:1–14, which includes Philip's request, “Lord, show us the Father.” Weekday readings of the Sixth Monday of Resurrection: 1 Peter 2:1–5; Matthew 23:23–28. The Latin calendar also keeps the feast of Sts Philip and James today (verify locally).
2027-05-03.verse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
theo: Today the Church honours two of the Twelve together, Philip and James. The Gospels tell us more about Philip than about many of the apostles, and almost all of it comes from John. Philip was “from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter” (John 1:44), a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus found him and said simply, “Follow me”, and Philip at once became a messenger: he found Nathanael and told him, “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus son of Joseph from Nazareth.” When Nathanael scoffed, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”, Philip did not argue; he said, “Come and see” (John 1:45–46). Before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus tested him: “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?”, and Philip, practical to the end, did the arithmetic: “Six months’ wages would not buy enough bread for each of them to get a little” (John 6:5–7). When some Greeks came to the feast and said, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus”, it was to Philip that they came (John 12:21). An early tradition, recorded by the historian Eusebius from a letter of Bishop Polycrates of Ephesus at the end of the second century, says that Philip was buried at Hierapolis in Asia Minor. The second apostle is James, the son of Alphaeus (Matthew 10:3). The Latin tradition has long identified him with James ‘the less’ and with James ‘the brother of the Lord’, who led the Church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19) and to whom the risen Lord appeared (1 Corinthians 15:7); the Eastern tradition has generally distinguished these figures. We need not settle the question to honour him: an apostle chosen by Christ, a witness of the Resurrection, and a pillar of the first Church. The two have been honoured together in the West since the dedication of the Basilica of the Holy Apostles in Rome, where their relics are kept, in the sixth century.

The Gospel of the feast is the conversation of the Last Supper in which Philip spoke. Jesus begins with words that Christians have read at countless deathbeds: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.” He is going to prepare a place, and he will come again and take us to himself, “so that where I am, there you may be also.” Thomas, honest as always, objects: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” And Jesus gives the answer that sums up the whole Gospel: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” In the longer reading, Philip asks the question that lies under every human search for God: “Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.” Jesus answers with gentle sorrow: “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” Three days before the Ascension these words take on a special weight. Jesus is going to the Father; but he is not leaving a map, he is leaving himself. The way to the Father is not a technique or a set of rules but a Person, the Son made man. The Church in India lives among many sincere seekers who speak of many paths to God. We honour every true search, for God is at work in it; but we cannot keep silent about the One who said, ‘I am the way.’

The two Old Testament readings sing of the victory God gives his faithful ones. Exodus gives the song of Moses on the shore of the sea, which the Church sings in the night of Easter: “I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. The Lord is my strength and my might, and he has become my salvation.” The apostles saw a greater exodus: the Lord passing through death and bringing his people out of the slavery of sin. Wisdom then describes the day when the despised righteous will be vindicated: “Then the righteous will stand with great confidence in the presence of those who have oppressed them and those who make light of their labors.” Their persecutors will say in amazement, “Why have they been numbered among the children of God? And why is their lot among the saints?” Tradition remembers that both Philip and James gave their lives for Christ. James, the brother of the Lord, was put to death in Jerusalem in the early sixties of the first century, as the Jewish historian Josephus records; of Philip's death the accounts are later and differ. The world thought their lives were wasted. The Church sings with Moses that the Lord has triumphed in them.

In the Epistle Paul explains why an apostle cannot be silent: “If I proclaim the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for an obligation is laid on me, and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!” He makes himself “a slave to all” so that he might win more of them; to Jews he becomes as a Jew, to those outside the law as one outside the law, to the weak weak: “I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.” This is not compromise of the truth but the humility of love, which goes to people where they are. Philip lived it when he said, “Come and see”, and when he brought the Greeks to Jesus. The weekday readings of this Sixth Monday add a word for us all. Peter calls the baptised “living stones” built into “a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ”, and in Matthew Jesus warns against a religion that is only outward, cleaning “the outside of the cup” while the inside stays unclean. The apostles' faith was not a show. It was a life given. On their feast we ask for that same apostolic faith, the faith of the Church that is built on the foundation of the apostles, and for the courage to say to our friends, as Philip did, ‘Come and see.’
conn: Come and see.
Philip's first act as a disciple is to bring a friend: “Philip said to him, ‘Come and see’” (John 1:46).
We wish to see Jesus.
The Greeks come to Philip: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus” (John 12:21).
Show me your glory.
Moses asked, “Show me your glory, I pray” (Exodus 33:18); Philip asks, “Lord, show us the Father” (John 14:8).
He appeared to James.
Paul lists the witnesses of the Resurrection: “Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:7).
James at the council.
At the council of Jerusalem James says, “My brothers, listen to me” (Acts 15:13), and helps the Church welcome the Gentiles.
The song of the sea.
The song of Moses returns in the heavenly liturgy: those who conquered sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).
Twelve foundations.
“And the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them are the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:14).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana we profess that the Church is apostolic. The faith we receive at the altar is the faith of Philip and James, handed down from the apostles to our own Mar Thoma and to us.
Philip asked, “Show us the Father.” At the altar the Son shows us the Father by giving himself: whoever receives him with faith is drawn into the life of the Father and the Son.
outline: Opening
Two apostles, a practical man from Bethsaida and a pillar of Jerusalem.
Point 1 · Lord, show us the Father
Philip's question and Jesus' answer.
Point 2 · I am the way, and the truth, and the life
No map, but a Person.
Point 3 · Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel
All things to all people.
Point 4 · The righteous will stand with confidence
The song of victory and the witness of the martyrs.
Closing image
A young man inviting his friend to the parish adoration: ‘Come and see.’
Take-home line
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
live: Say ‘Come and see’ (John 1:46)
Invite one friend this week to Holy Qurbana, adoration or a prayer meeting.
Seek the Father in the Son (John 14:9)
Spend ten minutes today looking at a crucifix or an icon of Christ, praying: Lord, show me the Father.
Inside the cup (Matthew 23:26)
Examine one area where your faith is only outward, and ask the Lord to cleanse it.
Pray for the apostolic faith
Pray the Nicene Creed slowly today, thanking God for the faith of the apostles.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
Christ as God is the homeland to which we are going; Christ as man is the way by which we go. We go to him through him, and we cannot get lost, because the way itself is walking with us.
St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

The glory of God is a human being fully alive, and the life of human beings is the vision of God. If the revelation of God through creation gives life, much more does the manifestation of the Father through the Word give life to those who see God.
magis: Catechism 516
Christ's whole earthly life is a revelation of the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father”.
Catechism 2466
In Jesus Christ the whole of God's truth has been made manifest; he is the truth, and whoever follows him lives in the Spirit of truth.
Catechism 857

The Church is apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles, keeping and handing on their teaching, and taught, sanctified and guided by the apostles until Christ's return through their successors.
Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate 2
The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions; yet she proclaims, and must ever proclaim, Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life.
saints: Today
Sts Philip and James, Apostles, in the First Set calendar; also in the Latin calendar today.
This week

1–6 May: the last days of the Resurrection season before the Ascension, in the month of May that our families dedicate to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Sat 1: St Joseph, Patron of the Working Class (May Day). Sun 2: Sixth Sunday of Resurrection; St Athanasius (2 May) gives way to the Sunday. Mon 3: Sts Philip and James, Apostles. Thu 6: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, an important feast and a day of obligation; St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May (verify locally).
2027-05-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the way, the truth and the life, and whoever sees you sees the Father. On the feast of your apostles Philip and James, keep us in the faith they proclaimed and sealed with their lives. Calm our troubled hearts, show us the Father, and give us the courage to say to our friends, Come and see. Make us living stones in your Church, clean within and without, until we reach the dwelling place you have gone to prepare for us. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-04.title: Sixth Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-05-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: New heavens and a new earth
2027-05-04.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Two days before the Ascension.
2027-05-04.verse: Beware, keep alert; for you do not know when the time will come.
theo: Two days before the Ascension the Church gives us a Gospel about the Lord's return. Jesus is speaking on the Mount of Olives, the very hill from which Luke says he will be taken up (Acts 1:12). “But about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” The saying has puzzled readers from the beginning: how can the Son not know? The Church's answer is careful. Jesus is truly God and truly man; in his human knowledge he knew all that he came to reveal, and he says plainly that the day of judgment is not among the things he was sent to make known (Catechism 474). The point of the saying is practical, not speculative: “Beware, keep alert; for you do not know when the time will come.” Then a little parable. A man goes on a journey, “puts his slaves in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to be on the watch.” Each has his work; none is idle; one stands at the door. That is the Church after the Ascension. The Master has gone; the house is in our hands; every member has a task, and all must watch.

Jesus names the four watches of the night: “for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or at dawn, or else he may find you asleep when he comes suddenly.” Mark's first readers would have noticed something. Only a few days later, on the night of the Passion, those same hours come one after another: in the evening the Supper; at midnight the agony in Gethsemane, where the disciples fall asleep three times; at cockcrow Peter's denial; at dawn Jesus handed over to Pilate. The disciples failed to keep awake on that night. After the Resurrection and the gift of the Spirit they learned to watch, and the Church has kept the night watches ever since in her prayer. In the Syro-Malabar tradition the Liturgy of the Hours, the Yamangal, keeps the rhythm of evening, night and morning prayer; the Night Prayer (Lelya) has a vigil character, and in many families the evening prayer before the crucifix still keeps the household awake to the Lord. The last word is for everyone: “And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”

The Second Letter of Peter tells us what we are waiting for. “But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a loud noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fire, and the earth and everything that is done on it will be disclosed.” The language is the vivid language of the prophets, and its point is moral: “Since all these things are to be dissolved in this way, what sort of persons ought you to be in leading lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God”. We can hasten it, Peter says, by holy lives, by prayer, by spreading the Gospel. And then the promise: “But, in accordance with his promise, we wait for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.” The Church teaches that the universe itself will be renewed and transformed, not thrown away (Catechism 1042–1047). Kerala has seen in recent years how fragile our hills and rivers are, in floods and landslides that took homes and lives. The Christian who waits for a new earth does not despise this one; he cares for it as a steward who will give an account, and longs for the day when righteousness will be at home everywhere. Every Holy Qurbana is celebrated in this waiting: we proclaim the Lord's death “until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26), and the early Church's prayer, Maranatha, Our Lord, come, is still on our lips.
outline: Opening
On the Mount of Olives, two days before the Ascension.
Point 1 · No one knows the day
The Master gone on a journey, and each with his work.
Point 2 · Evening, midnight, cockcrow, dawn
The hours of the Passion and the Church's night watch.
Point 3 · New heavens and a new earth
Holy lives that hasten the day of God.
Take-home line
“And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”
live: Do your work faithfully (Mark 13:34)
Do today's duty well, as a servant left in charge of the Master's house.
Keep a night watch (Mark 13:35)
Before sleeping tonight, pray for a few minutes for those who will die this night.
Care for the earth (2 Peter 3:13)
Do one practical thing this week to care for creation: save water, plant a tree, or avoid plastic.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

The Lord hid the hour of his coming so that we would keep watch. He did not reveal it, so that each generation might think that he will come in its own days. If he had revealed it, his coming would be an empty thing; because it is hidden, all ages are kept awake.
St Augustine (in substance)

The last day is hidden so that every day may be watched. Let each one fear lest his own last day find him unprepared; for as each one is found on the day he leaves this world, so will he be found on the last day.
magis: Catechism 474
In his human knowledge Christ knew fully the eternal plans he came to reveal; what he said he did not know in this matter, he elsewhere declared he was not sent to reveal.
Catechism 673
Since the Ascension Christ's coming in glory has been imminent, though it is not for us to know the times or seasons fixed by the Father.
Catechism 1042–1043
At the end of time the Kingdom of God will come in its fullness; Scripture calls this mysterious renewal new heavens and a new earth.
Catechism 1403
At the Last Supper the Lord turned his disciples' minds toward the fulfilment of the Passover in the Kingdom; the Church prays in her liturgy, Maranatha, Come, Lord Jesus.
2027-05-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you have gone to the Father and left your house in our hands. Keep us awake and faithful, each at the work you have given us. Do not let your coming find us asleep, in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or at dawn. Make us holy and godly as we wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home, and keep the prayer of your Church alive on our lips: Maranatha, come, Lord Jesus. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: Every Holy Qurbana proclaims the Lord's death until he comes. At the altar the Church stands like the doorkeeper of the parable, awake, waiting for the Master, and already receiving him in the Mysteries.

2027-05-05.title: Sixth Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-05-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Be imitators of God, as beloved children
2027-05-05.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Tomorrow, Thursday 6 May, is the feast of the Ascension of our Lord, a day of obligation; the evening prayer of today already belongs to the feast in many parishes (verify locally).
2027-05-05.verse: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”
theo: On the eve of the Ascension the Church gives us words from the Last Supper, words of a friend who is about to go away. “I have said these things to you so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete.” Jesus speaks of joy at the very hour when he is about to suffer. His joy is not the absence of trouble; it is the joy of the Son who knows himself loved by the Father and who loves to the end. He wants that joy in us, and he tells us where it is found: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” The measure is not our feelings or our convenience but his own love: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.” Tomorrow we will see him go up into heaven. Before he goes, he reminds us that the proof of his love was the Cross, and that the only way to remain in his joy is to love in the same way.

Then comes a word that every Christian should hear as addressed to himself: “I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.” In the Old Testament only a few were called friends of God: Abraham (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23) and Moses, with whom the Lord spoke “face to face, as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Now Jesus gives that name to fishermen and tax collectors, and through them to us. And he adds: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last”. Friendship with Christ is not a private consolation; it sends us out. The disciples would understand this after the Ascension and Pentecost, when the friends of Jesus became his witnesses to the ends of the earth. It is worth asking, on this eve: do I relate to Christ as a slave who obeys from fear, or as a friend who knows the Master's heart and shares his work?

Paul's letter to the Ephesians draws the practical conclusion: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.” Children imitate the parents they love; beloved children of God learn to love as he loves. Then Paul becomes very concrete. Sexual impurity and greed “must not even be mentioned among you, as is proper among saints”, and “Entirely out of place is obscene, silly, and vulgar talk; but instead, let there be thanksgiving.” In our time much obscene and vulgar talk passes through the screens in our hands, in jokes forwarded in groups and in what is watched in secret. Paul's remedy is not only a list of things to avoid but a positive habit: thanksgiving. A heart that thanks God is slow to soil itself. Greed, Paul adds, is a form of idolatry, the worship of things in place of God. On the eve of the Ascension we lift our eyes to the One who goes up to the Father, and we let him lift our hearts from what is low to what lasts: love, purity and gratitude.
outline: Opening
The eve of the Ascension: the words of a friend about to go away.
Point 1 · That your joy may be complete
Love one another as I have loved you.
Point 2 · I have called you friends
Chosen and sent to bear fruit that will last.
Point 3 · Imitators of God
Love, purity and thanksgiving.
Take-home line
“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”
live: Love as he loved (John 15:12)
Do one hidden act of self-giving love today for someone who cannot repay you.
Speak as a friend (John 15:15)
Spend ten minutes tonight speaking to Jesus as a friend, telling him about your day.
Replace vulgar talk with thanks (Ephesians 5:4)
Delete or refuse to forward one unworthy message today, and thank God for three gifts instead.
fathers: St Aelred of Rievaulx (in substance)
Here we are, you and I, and I hope that Christ is the third among us. Friendship that begins in Christ, grows according to Christ and is perfected in Christ is a stairway to the friendship of God.
St Augustine (in substance)
Blessed is the one who loves you, Lord, and his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. Such a one never loses anyone dear to him, for all are dear in the One who is never lost.
magis: Catechism 1823
Jesus makes charity the new commandment: by loving his own to the end, he shows the Father's love which he receives, and by loving one another the disciples imitate the love of Jesus.
Catechism 2347
The virtue of chastity blossoms in friendship; it shows the disciple how to follow and imitate him who has chosen us as his friends.
Catechism 2637
Thanksgiving characterises the prayer of the Church, which in celebrating the Eucharist reveals and becomes more fully what she is.
2027-05-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the eve of your Ascension you call us your friends and give us your commandment of love. Let your joy be in us and make our joy complete. Teach us to love as you have loved us, to the laying down of our lives. Keep our hearts and our words clean, and fill our mouths with thanksgiving. You chose us: send us to bear fruit that will last, and tomorrow lift our hearts with you to the Father. Amen. Alleluia!
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the fragrant offering of which Paul speaks: Christ who loved us and gave himself up for us. Here the Friend lays down his life and gives it to us as food, so that we may love one another as he has loved us.

2027-05-07.title: Sixth Friday of Resurrection · First Friday
2027-05-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The one who comes from above is above all
2027-05-07.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The day after the Ascension of our Lord, and the First Friday of the month, kept with devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Many begin today the novena to the Holy Spirit, the nine days of prayer that lead to Pentecost.
2027-05-07.verse: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
theo: Yesterday the Church celebrated the Ascension of our Lord. The disciples stood on the Mount of Olives looking up, and two men in white asked them, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” (Acts 1:11). Then they went back to Jerusalem, to the upper room, and began to pray. Today's Gospel is a commentary on what they had just seen. “The one who comes from above is above all; the one who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks about earthly things. The one who comes from heaven is above all.” These words, at the end of the third chapter of John, describe Jesus as the One who came down from the Father; after the Ascension we hear them also as a description of the One who has gone back up. He came from above, and he has returned above. He is not one teacher among many, not a holy man who rose a little higher than the rest of us: he is the One who is above all. That is why the Church can call him Lord, and why the Holy Qurbana is offered to him and through him to the Father. The Gospel adds a sad line: “yet no one accepts his testimony.” But it also adds a promise: “Whoever has accepted his testimony has certified this, that God is true.” Every act of faith is a little seal pressed on the truth of God.

Then comes the verse that opens the nine days before Pentecost: “He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.” The prophets received the Spirit for a time and for a task. The Son receives the Spirit without measure, and he gives the Spirit without measure. Before he went to the Father he had promised, “if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). The Ascension is not an absence; it is the condition of the gift. So the disciples do not sit idle in the upper room. They pray, “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). The Church has always seen in those days the first novena, nine days of prayer with the Mother of the Lord, waiting for the Spirit who would make them a Church. The Gospel closes with the Father's love: “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.” The hands that were nailed to the Cross now hold all things. On this First Friday we look also at the pierced side of the same Lord: from his open Heart came blood and water (John 19:34), and from that Heart the Spirit is poured out.

Paul writes to the Philippians as a man who has met that Lord and cannot stand still. “Not that I have already obtained this or have already reached the goal; but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.” Paul does not boast of what he has reached. He speaks like a runner in the last lap: “forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus.” The Greek words behind “the heavenly call” can mean “the upward call”: God calls us upward, where Christ has gone before us. The Ascension gives our whole life a direction. We do not run in circles; we run toward the place where our Head has already arrived. And Paul adds a gentle word for those who see things differently: “if you think differently about anything, this too God will reveal to you.” The one who runs toward Christ is patient with fellow runners. The novena begins today: let it be nine days of running toward the Lord, forgetting the failures behind us, and asking the Father for the Spirit who is given without measure.
conn: Why do you stand looking up?
At the Ascension the two men in white said, “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).
The Spirit after the glory.
“Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.” John adds: “as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:38–39).
The pierced side.
“One of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34); the Church sees here the birth of the sacraments from the Heart of Christ.
The waiting with Mary.
“All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14).
They shall run.
“Those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary” (Isaiah 40:31).
Seek the things above.
“So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who has gone up to the Father comes down to us in his Body and Blood. He is above all, and yet he lets himself be held in our hands. From the altar, as from his pierced Heart, flow the blood and water of the sacraments.

On this First Friday many receive Holy Communion in reparation and love, as the Lord asked through St Margaret Mary. Receive him today with a heart that is straining forward, asking him for the Spirit.
outline: Opening
The day after the Ascension: disciples who stop looking up and start praying.
Point 1 · The One from above is above all
The Ascended Lord, his testimony, and our seal on the truth of God.
Point 2 · He gives the Spirit without measure
The first novena, with Mary in the upper room, and the open Heart of Jesus.
Point 3 · I press on toward the goal
The upward call: the Ascension gives our life a direction.
Closing image
A relay runner who forgets the stumble on the first bend and runs toward the hand stretched out at the finish.
Take-home line
“He gives the Spirit without measure.”
live: Begin the novena (Acts 1:14)
Pray each day until Pentecost: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.” Pray it with Mary, asking her to pray with you.
Make the First Friday (John 19:34)
Go to confession and receive Holy Communion today if you can, and spend a few minutes before the Sacred Heart.
Forget what lies behind (Philippians 3:13)
Name one failure you keep returning to, place it in the Heart of Jesus, and decide not to carry it into these nine days.
Accept his testimony (John 3:33)
Read one page of the Gospel slowly today and say at the end: Lord, I believe that you speak the words of God.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Christ has ascended into heaven: let our hearts ascend with him. He is there, and yet he is still with us here; we are here, and yet we are already with him there. He by his divinity, his power and his love; we by love, though not yet in body.
St Gregory of Nyssa (in substance)

Paul, who had been caught up to the third heaven, still says that he strains forward. To find God is to go on seeking him; the desire for God is never filled up and ended, because God has no limit. The soul that loves him always rises higher.
magis: Catechism 665–667

The Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain. As Head of the Church he precedes us, so that we, his members, may live in the hope of one day being with him for ever; there he intercedes for us.
Catechism 729
Only when the hour has arrived for his glorification does Jesus promise the coming of the Holy Spirit, since his death and Resurrection will fulfil the promise made to the fathers.
Catechism 965
After her Son's Ascension, Mary aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers: with the apostles and the women, she implored by her prayers the gift of the Spirit.
Catechism 478

Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion, and gave himself up for each one of us. The Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the chief sign and symbol of that love.
saints: This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came from above and you have returned to the Father; you are above all, and all things are placed in your hands. As your disciples waited in the upper room with Mary your Mother, we wait for the Spirit whom you give without measure. Open the treasures of your Sacred Heart to us on this First Friday; make us forget what lies behind and run toward the upward call of God. Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-08.title: Sixth Saturday of Resurrection
2027-05-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire
2027-05-08.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The second day of the novena to the Holy Spirit; a Saturday in the Marian month of May.
2027-05-08.verse: I baptize you with water for repentance, but one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
theo: Between the Ascension and Pentecost the Church takes us back to the banks of the Jordan, to the first promise of the Spirit in the Gospel. John the Baptist sees many Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism, and he speaks with the bluntness of a prophet: “Bear fruit worthy of repentance.” He is not condemning a whole people; he is speaking to religious leaders of his own nation, as the prophets of Israel always did, and his words strike every religious person in every age, ourselves first. He warns them against a comfortable security: “Do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our ancestor’; for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.” A Christian can say the same kind of thing: I was baptised as a child, my family has been Catholic since the time of St Thomas, our parish is ancient. All true, and all precious. But none of it replaces the fruit of a converted life. “Even now the ax is lying at the root of the trees.” The time is short, and God looks for fruit, not for family trees.

Then John points away from himself: “I baptize you with water for repentance, but one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Water washes; fire transforms. John's baptism prepared the heart; the baptism of Jesus gives the Spirit himself. That promise is fulfilled at Pentecost, when “divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:3–4). In these nine days we pray for that fire. It is not a fire that destroys the person; it burns away the chaff and leaves the wheat. “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and will gather his wheat into the granary.” A Kerala farmer who has seen paddy winnowed in the wind knows the picture: the light husk flies away, the heavy grain falls at his feet. The Spirit does in us what the wind does on the threshing floor. What is empty in us is blown away; what is good is gathered into God's granary.

Paul speaks to the Corinthians about another kind of fruit: a heart given entirely to the Lord. “The unmarried man is anxious about the affairs of the Lord, how to please the Lord; but the married man is anxious about the affairs of the world, how to please his wife, and his interests are divided.” Paul is not despising marriage; in the same letter he calls marriage a gift from God (1 Corinthians 7:7), and the Church honours it as a sacrament. He is speaking of a particular call, celibacy for the sake of the kingdom, which lets a person belong to the Lord with an undivided heart. His purpose is clear: “I say this for your own benefit, not to put any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and unhindered devotion to the Lord.” Every Christian, married or not, is called to that undivided devotion in his or her own state of life. On this Saturday of May we look to the Virgin Mary, whose heart was never divided: she belonged wholly to God, and she was also the most devoted of mothers. In the upper room she prayed with the apostles for the Spirit who had come upon her at Nazareth (Luke 1:35). Let us ask her to obtain for us, in this novena, the fire that makes the heart whole.
conn: The Spirit and fire at Pentecost.
“Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:3–4).
The refiner's fire.
“For he is like a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap” (Malachi 3:2): the Lord purifies his people as gold is purified.
Children of Abraham.
Paul writes, “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).
The tree and its fruit.
Jesus repeats John's warning: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:19–20).
The Spirit overshadowing Mary.
“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).
Eunuchs for the kingdom.
Jesus speaks of those who renounce marriage “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the priest calls down the Holy Spirit in the epiclesis, that he may come and dwell on the offering. The fire John promised comes to rest on the bread and wine, and through them on us.

Those who serve the altar with an undivided heart, priests and religious, are a gift to the Church. Pray for them at this Qurbana, and offer your own heart, in whatever state of life, without division.
outline: Opening
From the Ascension back to the Jordan: the first promise of the Spirit.
Point 1 · Bear fruit worthy of repentance
Family trees are precious, but God looks for fruit.
Point 2 · The Holy Spirit and fire
Water washes, fire transforms; the winnowing of the heart.
Point 3 · Unhindered devotion to the Lord
Celibacy for the kingdom, the holiness of marriage, and the undivided heart of Mary.
Closing image
Paddy winnowed in the wind on a threshing floor in Kuttanad.
Take-home line
“He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”
live: Name one fruit (Matthew 3:8)
Choose one concrete fruit of conversion for this week: a reconciliation, an apology, an honest account.
Pray for the fire (Matthew 3:11)
In the novena today, ask the Holy Spirit to burn away one habit that is only chaff in your life.
An undivided hour (1 Corinthians 7:35)
Give the Lord one hour this weekend with nothing else in your hands: no phone, no work, only prayer.
Pray for vocations
Pray a decade of the rosary today with Mary for priests, religious and families, that their hearts may be undivided.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

The Lord baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire because the grace of the Spirit is like fire: it burns away the thorns of sin and makes the soul shine, as iron placed in the fire takes on its glow. What fire does to iron, the Spirit does to the soul that receives him.
St Ambrose (in substance)

Let the life of the Virgin Mary be set before you like a picture, in which, as in a mirror, the beauty of chastity and the form of every virtue shine. From her we learn what to correct, what to imitate and what to hold fast.
magis: Catechism 696

Fire symbolizes the transforming energy of the Holy Spirit's actions. John the Baptist proclaims Christ as the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire; in the form of tongues as of fire the Spirit rests on the disciples at Pentecost.
Catechism 1427–1429
Jesus calls to conversion. This call is addressed first to those who do not yet know Christ, and also to Christians, for whom conversion is an uninterrupted task for the whole Church.
Catechism 1618–1620

Christ is the centre of all Christian life. Virginity for the sake of the kingdom of heaven is an unfolding of baptismal grace; both the sacrament of Matrimony and virginity for the kingdom come from the Lord himself, and they reinforce each other.
Catechism 506
Mary is a virgin because her virginity is the sign of her faith unadulterated by any doubt, and of her undivided gift of herself to God's will.
saints: This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, more powerful than John, you baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. In these days of waiting, burn away the chaff in our hearts and gather the wheat into your granary. Keep us from trusting in our name or our history; make us bear fruit worthy of repentance. Give to your priests and religious undivided hearts, and to our families a devotion to you that nothing can divide. Through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, whose heart was wholly yours, send us your Spirit at Pentecost. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-10.title: Seventh Monday of Resurrection
2027-05-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God chose you as the first fruits for salvation
2027-05-10.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The fourth day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. In the Latin calendar, St John of Avila, priest and doctor of the Church (optional memorial).
2027-05-10.verse: The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.
theo: It is noon in Samaria. “Jesus, tired out by his journey, was sitting by the well.” The Lord who has now ascended to the Father once sat tired on the edge of Jacob's well, in the heat of the day, and asked a woman for water: “Give me a drink.” She is astonished, for “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans”, and a Jewish teacher did not usually speak alone with a woman of Samaria. Jesus crosses both walls at once. He is not ashamed to need something from her. That is how God often begins with us: not with a command but with a request. He asks for a little of our time, a little of our attention, a cup of water, so that he can give far more. “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman thinks of running water from a spring rather than the still water of the cistern. Jesus means something deeper: the gift of God himself.

She objects with the practical sense of a woman who has carried water every day of her life: “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep.” And she asks the great question: “Are you greater than our ancestor Jacob?” Jesus answers by comparing two kinds of water. “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but those who drink of the water that I will give them will never be thirsty. The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.” John explains later what this water is: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive; for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:39). Now Jesus has been glorified. He has gone up to the Father, and the Spirit is about to be poured out. That is why we read this Gospel in the days of the novena. Every thirst we carry, for love, for meaning, for forgiveness, for peace, is in the end a thirst for God, and the Holy Spirit is the spring that God places inside us. The woman's first answer is still on the surface: “Sir, give me this water, so that I may never be thirsty or have to keep coming here to draw water.” But she has begun to ask, and the conversation that follows will make her the first missionary of her town.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians with gratitude, because the same Spirit has already been at work in them. “God chose you as the first fruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and through belief in the truth.” The first fruits were the first part of the harvest, offered to God as a promise of the rest. The young Church of Thessalonica was the first harvest in its city; the Syro-Malabar Church, born from the preaching of Thomas, was among the first fruits of the Gospel in India. Paul's advice to such a Church is simple: “So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by our letter.” The faith comes to us by the living voice of the Church and by the Scriptures together. Our Mar Thoma tradition, the prayers our grandparents taught us, the way our Church celebrates the Qurbana, are not dead customs; they are channels through which the living water has reached us. Paul ends with a blessing for these days of waiting: “may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and through grace gave us eternal comfort and good hope, comfort your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.”
conn: Jacob's well.
Jacob bought a plot of land at Shechem, and it became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants (Genesis 33:18–20; Joshua 24:32); Jesus meets the woman at the well of the patriarchs.
Wells of salvation.
“With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3).
The fountain of living water.
“They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug out cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).
I thirst.
On the Cross the One who offered living water says, “I am thirsty” (John 19:28).
Rivers of living water.
“Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.” John explains: “Now he said this about the Spirit” (John 7:38–39).
Let everyone who is thirsty come.
“And let everyone who is thirsty come. Let anyone who wishes take the water of life as a gift” (Revelation 22:17).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who asked for a drink at the well gives us himself to drink: his Blood is the living water that becomes in us a spring gushing up to eternal life.
We bring to the altar our tiredness and our thirst, as the woman brought her empty jar, and we take home the Spirit who comforts and strengthens our hearts.
outline: Opening
Noon at Jacob's well: the tired Lord asks a woman for water.
Point 1 · Give me a drink
God begins with a request, and crosses every wall.
Point 2 · Living water
The Spirit, the spring inside us, poured out after the Ascension.
Point 3 · Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions
First fruits, Mar Thoma heritage, and the eternal comfort of God.
Closing image
An old family well in a Kerala courtyard that never dried, even in a hard summer.
Take-home line
“The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.”
live: Name your thirst (John 4:15)
In the novena today, tell the Lord honestly what you are thirsty for, and ask him for the living water of the Spirit.
Cross one wall (John 4:9)
Speak kindly this week with someone your family or community usually keeps at a distance.
Hold fast to the traditions (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
Teach a child one prayer of our Church this week, or explain one part of the Qurbana.
Give a drink
Offer water or a cool drink to a delivery worker, a labourer or a guest today, in the name of Christ.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

He who asked for a drink was thirsting for her faith. He asked for water and promised water; he asked as one in need, and he promised as one who could fill her. He came tired to the well, he who is the strength of the weak, so that he might find the one who was lost.
St Irenaeus (in substance)

The tradition of the apostles, made known throughout the whole world, can be found in every Church by those who wish to see the truth. The Church, like a rich storehouse, has received from the apostles all that belongs to the truth, so that whoever will may draw from her the water of life.
magis: Catechism 2560–2561
Jesus thirsts; his asking arises from the depths of God's desire for us. Whether we realize it or not, prayer is the encounter of God's thirst with ours. God thirsts that we may thirst for him.
Catechism 694
Water signifies the Holy Spirit's action in Baptism. The Spirit is also personally the living water welling up from Christ crucified as its source and welling up in us to eternal life.
Catechism 78 and 80–82

The living transmission accomplished in the Holy Spirit is called Tradition. Tradition and Scripture are bound closely together: flowing from the same divine wellspring, they make up a single sacred deposit of the faith.

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, tired from your journey you sat by the well and asked for a drink, so that you might give us the living water. Now you are glorified at the Father's right hand: pour out on us the Spirit you promised, and let him become in us a spring gushing up to eternal life. Satisfy our deepest thirst, help us to cross the walls that divide people, and keep us faithful to the traditions handed down to us from the apostles. Comfort our hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-11.title: Seventh Tuesday of Resurrection
2027-05-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Do not become a stumbling block to the weak
The parable of the rich fool
2027-05-11.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The fifth day of the novena to the Holy Spirit.
2027-05-11.verse: So it is with those who store up treasures for themselves but are not rich toward God.
theo: A man in the crowd interrupts Jesus with a family quarrel: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the family inheritance with me.” Anyone who has lived in Kerala knows how familiar that sentence sounds. A few cents of land, a share in the ancestral house, a dispute over who looked after the parents: brothers stop speaking, cousins go to court, and sometimes the quarrel outlives everyone who began it. Jesus refuses to become the judge of the case: “Friend, who set me to be a judge or arbitrator over you?” He is not indifferent to justice; he goes to the root of the problem: “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.” The word for life here is not the life of the body but life itself, the real life of a person. A house can be divided fairly and the heart still be poisoned by greed. Jesus wants to heal the heart.

Then he tells the parable of the rich man whose land produced abundantly. Notice how he speaks: “What should I do, for I have no place to store my crops?” “I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.” He talks only to himself. There is no one else in his plans: no God to thank, no neighbour to share with, no poor man at his gate. Then God speaks for the first time, and calls him by his true name: “You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” The answer is painfully simple: someone else's, perhaps the very brothers who will quarrel over them. Jesus ends: “So it is with those who store up treasures for themselves but are not rich toward God.” To be rich toward God is to let our goods pass through our hands into his: in thanksgiving, in almsgiving, in support for the Church and the poor. In these days before Pentecost, the Holy Spirit is the true treasure we ask for; and he is given not to those who fill their barns but to those who empty their hands.

Paul deals with a different question in Corinth, but the root is the same. Some Christians knew that idols are nothing, and so they ate meat sacrificed to idols without a second thought. Paul agrees that “food will not bring us close to God”. But he adds: “take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.” A believer whose conscience is still fragile might see a strong Christian eating in an idol's temple and be led back into idolatry. “So by your knowledge those weak believers for whom Christ died are destroyed.” The phrase cuts deep: the weak brother is one for whom Christ died. Knowledge that ignores him is not wisdom but pride; earlier in the same chapter Paul says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). His conclusion is generous: “Therefore, if food is a cause of their falling, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause one of them to fall.” Our rights, like our riches, are given us for others. A Christian who drinks heavily in front of a young person, who mocks the simple faith of an old woman, or who boasts of his knowledge while his neighbour stumbles, has forgotten that his brother is someone for whom Christ died.
conn: Vanity of vanities.
“The lover of money will not be satisfied with money; nor the lover of wealth, with gain. This also is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 5:10).
Naked I came.
“Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return there” (Job 1:21).
Treasure in heaven.
“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust consume … but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:19–20).
The stumbling block.
“You shall not revile the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).
Woe to the one who causes stumbling.
Jesus warns against causing one of the little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
Love builds up.
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1); “Let all that you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16:14).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we bring our offerings to the altar: a sign that what we have is not only for our barns but for God and for the poor. The Lord who gave his life for the weak gives himself to us, and makes us rich toward God.
At Communion we receive the Body of Christ together with the weakest members of the parish. Let us look at them as brothers and sisters for whom Christ died.
outline: Opening
A family quarrel over an inheritance, and Jesus who goes to the root.
Point 1 · Life does not consist in possessions
Greed, the poison that a fair division cannot cure.
Point 2 · You fool! This very night
The man who talked only to himself, and being rich toward God.
Point 3 · Do not become a stumbling block
Knowledge puffs up, love builds up; the weak brother for whom Christ died.
Closing image
Two brothers in Kottayam who sold the disputed plot and built a house for a poor family instead.
Take-home line
“Not rich toward God.”
live: Make peace over property (Luke 12:13)
If there is a quarrel over land or inheritance in your family, take one step toward peace this week: a call, a visit, a compromise.
Empty one barn (Luke 12:18)
Give away something you have stored and do not use: clothes, money, food, time.
Be rich toward God (Luke 12:21)
Set aside a fixed share of your income for God and the poor, and give it with joy.
Protect the weak (1 Corinthians 8:9)
Avoid one habit, a drink, a joke, a careless word, that could make a younger or weaker person stumble.
fathers: St Basil the Great (in substance)

Whom do I wrong, you say, by keeping what is mine? The bread you hold back belongs to the hungry; the coat you store in your chest belongs to the naked; the shoes rotting in your house belong to the barefoot; the money you hide away belongs to the needy. You wrong as many as you could have helped.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Not to share our own goods with the poor is to rob them and to take away their life. The goods we possess are not ours but theirs. Do not say, I use what is mine; you use what belongs to others, for all good things come from God and are given us to be shared.
magis: Catechism 2536
The tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit; it forbids avarice arising from a passion for riches and their attendant power.
Catechism 2446
St John Chrysostom vigorously recalls this: “Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life. The goods we possess are not ours, but theirs.”
Catechism 2284–2287
Scandal is an attitude or behaviour which leads another to do evil. It is grave when given by those who by nature or office are obliged to teach and educate others; Jesus utters a curse against it.
Catechism 1790
A human being must always obey the certain judgement of his conscience; conscience must be informed and moral judgement enlightened.
saints: This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you became poor for our sake, so that by your poverty we might become rich. Guard us against every kind of greed. Heal the quarrels in our families over land and money, and teach us that our life does not consist in our possessions. Make us rich toward God by sharing what we have with the poor. Give us a love that builds up, so that we never cause a weaker brother or sister to stumble, remembering that you died for them. Send us your Holy Spirit, the true treasure, and fill our empty hands. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-12.title: Seventh Wednesday of Resurrection
2027-05-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God is love; he has given us of his Spirit
This is eternal life: that they may know you
2027-05-12.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The sixth day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. In the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus, martyrs, and St Pancras, martyr (optional memorials).
2027-05-12.verse: And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
theo: On the night before he died, at the end of the Last Supper, Jesus lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed aloud before his disciples. The Church calls this prayer, which fills the seventeenth chapter of John, the prayer of the Hour or the high-priestly prayer. “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you.” The hour is the hour of the Cross, and Jesus calls it glory. On the Cross the love of the Father and the Son is shown to the world, and through the Cross the Son returns to the glory he had “before the world existed”. We read this prayer in the days after the Ascension because the prayer has been answered: the Son has been glorified and has gone back to the Father. But the prayer has not ended. The Letter to the Hebrews says that the Risen Lord “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). What Jesus prayed in the upper room he goes on praying at the Father's right hand, and in these nine days the Church in the upper room joins her prayer to his.

At the centre of the prayer is a definition: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” Eternal life is not first of all a long life after death; it is a relationship that begins now. In the Bible to know someone is more than to know facts about him; it is to love him, to share his life, as husband and wife know each other. So eternal life is to know the Father and the Son in the love of the Holy Spirit. A child preparing for First Holy Communion who learns to talk to Jesus has begun eternal life. An old grandmother saying her rosary in the evening is living it. Jesus adds, “I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.” His whole life was obedience, and that obedience is his glory. We too glorify God not by great deeds but by doing faithfully the work he gives us, in the kitchen, the classroom, the hospital ward, the field.

The First Letter of John shows what that knowledge looks like in practice. “No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.” We cannot see God, but we can see our brother, and in loving him the invisible God becomes present. Then comes the link with Pentecost: “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” The Spirit is the gift that makes this love possible. John puts it in words that sum up the whole Gospel: “God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them.” And he draws a bold consequence: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear.” Many Christians live with a fearful religion, afraid of God as of a harsh judge. John says that the closer we come to God's love, the less room fear has. But he will not let us escape into sweet feelings: “Those who say, ‘I love God,’ and hate their brothers or sisters, are liars.” On this day of the novena we ask the Spirit for a love that is real: love that casts out fear before God and love that reaches the brother we can see.
conn: Everlasting love.
“I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you” (Jeremiah 31:3).
The knowledge of God.
“For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6).
He always intercedes.
“Consequently he is able for all time to save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
The glory before the world.
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1); “we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son” (John 1:14).
God's love poured out.
“God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).
Fear not.
“Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God” (Isaiah 41:10).
altar: The prayer of John 17 was spoken at the table of the Last Supper. In every Holy Qurbana the Lord who prayed that night offers himself to the Father, and the Church prays with him and through him, in the Holy Spirit.
In Communion we come to know him in the deepest way: not only by hearing about him but by receiving him. Let that knowledge become love for the brothers and sisters who receive him beside us.
outline: Opening
The night before he died, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays.
Point 1 · Father, the hour has come
The Cross as glory, and the High Priest who still intercedes.
Point 2 · This is eternal life
To know the Father and the Son: a relationship that begins now.
Point 3 · God is love; perfect love casts out fear
The Spirit's gift, the brother we can see, and a faith without fear.
Closing image
A grandmother in Changanacherry saying her rosary at dusk, at home with God.
Take-home line
“God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God.”
live: Pray with the High Priest (John 17:1)
Read John 17 slowly this week, a few verses each day, and join your prayer to the prayer of Jesus.
Know him, not only about him (John 17:3)
Spend ten minutes today speaking to Jesus as to a friend, before the Blessed Sacrament if you can.
Love the brother you can see (1 John 4:20)
Do one concrete act of love today for someone you find difficult.
Let love cast out fear (1 John 4:18)
Name one fear you carry before God, and entrust it to his love in the novena prayer.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you cry out, cry out out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within you; from this root nothing but good can grow.
St Irenaeus (in substance)

The glory of God is a human being fully alive, and the life of a human being is the vision of God. If the revelation of God through creation gives life to all who live on earth, how much more does the manifestation of the Father through the Word give life to those who see God.
magis: Catechism 221

St John goes even further when he affirms that “God is love”: God's very being is love. By sending his only Son and the Spirit of Love, God has revealed his innermost secret: God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Catechism 2746–2751

When his hour had come, Jesus prayed to the Father. His prayer, the longest transmitted by the Gospel, embraces the whole economy of creation and salvation; it is the prayer of our High Priest, inseparable from his sacrifice.
Catechism 1822–1829
Charity is the theological virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbour as ourselves for the love of God. It is the form of all the virtues.
saints: This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night of your Passion you lifted your eyes to heaven and prayed for us, and now at the Father's right hand you live for ever to intercede for us. Grant us eternal life: to know the Father, the only true God, and you whom he has sent. Pour into our hearts the Spirit of love, so that perfect love may cast out all fear, and we may love the brothers and sisters we can see. Let us glorify the Father by finishing the work he gives us each day. With Mary, who abode in your love, we pray: come, Holy Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-13.title: Seventh Thursday of Resurrection
2027-05-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: We declare to you the word of life
2027-05-13.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The seventh day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. In the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima (optional memorial), recalling the first apparition to three shepherd children at Fatima in Portugal on 13 May 1917.
