2027-05-13.verse: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
theo: The First Letter of John opens with a breathless sentence, the words of an old man who cannot forget what he saw as a young one: “We declare to you what was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and touched with our hands, concerning the word of life.” Heard, seen, looked at, touched: four verbs piled one on another. John insists that the faith rests on a real encounter with a real person. The Word who was with the Father from the beginning became flesh, ate with fishermen, invited Thomas to put his hand into his side. “This life was revealed, and we have seen it and testify to it.” Now the Lord has ascended and is no longer seen in that way. How then do we meet him? John answers: through the witness of the apostles, handed on in the Church. “We declare to you what we have seen and heard so that you also may have fellowship with us; and truly our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.” The chain is clear: the apostles saw; they declared; we who hear them enter into fellowship with them, and through them with the Father and the Son. Our Church received that witness from Thomas, the apostle who touched the wounds. In these days before Pentecost, the Spirit is preparing the apostles to begin declaring.

The Gospel shows what that fellowship costs. “Now large crowds were traveling with him; and he turned and said to them, ‘Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.’” The word “hate” shocks us. In the language of the Bible it is a way of saying “prefer less”; Matthew gives the same saying as “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Jesus is not asking us to stop loving our families; he who gave us the commandment to honour father and mother asks that no love, not even the dearest, take his place. Then he speaks plainly: “Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.” A crowd follows for a day; a disciple follows to the end.

Jesus gives two little parables of good sense. A man who wants to build a tower first sits down and estimates the cost, so that he is not mocked: “This fellow began to build and was not able to finish.” A king going to war with ten thousand against twenty thousand first sits down and considers whether he can win. Both sit down before they begin. Discipleship is not an enthusiasm of one evening; it is a decision taken with open eyes. “So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.” Finally he speaks of salt: “Salt is good; but if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored?” A disciple who has stopped paying the cost loses his flavour. Many in Kerala know what that means: families where the faith has become only a custom, where the name is Christian but the taste is gone. Salt, Leviticus says, was offered with every sacrifice as “the salt of the covenant” (Leviticus 2:13). Today the Latin Church remembers Our Lady of Fatima, who asked three poor children to pray, to do penance and to offer sacrifices for sinners. Mary is the disciple who counted the cost at Nazareth and paid it at the foot of the Cross. In the upper room she prayed for the Spirit who alone can give us the courage to finish the tower we have begun.
conn: The Word from the beginning.
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); “the Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14).
Touch me and see.
The Risen Lord says, “Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).
Thomas touches the wounds.
“Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side” (John 20:27).
Loving more than me.
“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).
Ruth's choice.
“Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).
Salt of the earth.
“You are the salt of the earth; but if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored?” (Matthew 5:13).
altar: The Word of life whom the apostles touched is placed in our hands at every Holy Qurbana. We too can say: we have received, we have touched, we have tasted. Our fellowship at the altar is fellowship with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
At the altar Christ carries his Cross to the end and offers himself fully; there we receive strength to carry our own cross and to keep the salt of our faith from losing its taste.
outline: Opening
An old apostle who cannot forget what he heard, saw and touched.
Point 1 · The word of life
Heard, seen, touched: the witness handed on to us from Thomas.
Point 2 · Carry the cross and follow me
No love in place of Christ; the crowd and the disciple.
Point 3 · Sit down and count the cost
The tower, the king, and the salt that keeps its taste.
Closing image
An unfinished house on a Kerala roadside, its pillars rusting in the rain.
Take-home line
“Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.”
live: Bear witness (1 John 1:3)
Tell one person this week, simply, what Jesus has done in your life.
Put Christ first (Luke 14:26)
Look at one family duty or affection that has pushed God aside, and give God his place again, without loving your family less.
Count the cost (Luke 14:28)
Choose one Christian commitment you have started and left half done, and decide how to finish it.
Keep the salt (Luke 14:34)
Restore one practice that has lost its taste in your home: family prayer, Sunday Qurbana, grace before meals.
Pray with Mary of Fatima
Pray the rosary today for the conversion of sinners and for peace, as Our Lady asked the children at Fatima.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

What does John mean when he says, our hands have touched the Word of life? Can anyone touch the Word with his hands? But because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, the Word who could not be touched became touchable. Through those who touched him we too have come to him.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The disciples are called salt not for their own sake but for the whole earth. Salt does not preserve itself; it preserves what it touches. If the salt loses its strength, it cannot preserve others, and it is fit only to be thrown away. So the Christian lives not for himself but to keep the world from corruption.
magis: Catechism 425

The transmission of the Christian faith consists primarily in proclaiming Jesus Christ in order to lead others to faith in him. From the beginning, the first disciples burned with the desire to proclaim Christ: “We cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.”
Catechism 2232
Family ties are important but not absolute. The first vocation of the Christian is to follow Jesus: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”
Catechism 1435
Conversion is accomplished in daily life by gestures of reconciliation, care for the poor and the defence of justice; taking up one's cross each day and following Jesus is the surest way of penance.
Catechism 782
The People of God has for its mission to be salt of the earth and light of the world.
Catechism 67
Private revelations, recognised by the Church, do not improve or complete Christ's definitive Revelation, but help us to live it more fully in a certain period of history.
saints: This week

7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-13.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Word of life, you were heard, seen and touched by your apostles, and through their witness we have fellowship with the Father and with you. Give us the courage to put you before every other love, to carry our cross and follow you to the end. Teach us to count the cost and to finish what we have begun, and keep the salt of our faith from losing its taste. Through the prayers of the Virgin Mary, who paid the cost of discipleship at the foot of the Cross and prayed with the apostles for the Spirit, send us your Holy Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-14.title: Seventh Friday of Resurrection · St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha)
2027-05-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The LORD looks on the heart: David is anointed
Matthias is added to the eleven apostles
God chose what is weak in the world
Revealed to infants; come to me and find rest
2027-05-14.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. These are the days between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the Church, like the apostles with Mary in the upper room, prays for the coming of the Holy Spirit. St Matthias the Apostle (the calendar spells the name Mathias) is listed in the First Set with the readings above; the calendar gives the longer form 1 Samuel 16:1–13. Weekday readings of the Seventh Friday: 1 John 2:22–25; Matthew 24:7–14. In the Latin calendar St Matthias is also kept today, as a feast. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-05-14.verse: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.
theo: Today the Church remembers an apostle about whom Scripture tells us one story only, and that story happens in these very days. Between the Ascension and Pentecost the eleven return to Jerusalem and go up to the upper room, and Luke tells us that “All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus, as well as his brothers” (Acts 1:14). The next verse begins: “In those days Peter stood up among the believers (together the crowd numbered about one hundred twenty persons)”. So the choice of Matthias is made by a praying Church, gathered around the Mother of the Lord, waiting for the Spirit. Peter, who had denied his Master three times and been forgiven by the lakeshore, now acts as the shepherd Jesus made him. He does not hide the painful wound: Judas “was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” The place left empty by betrayal must be filled, because the Twelve are not a random committee. Jesus had chosen twelve, as Israel had twelve tribes, and had promised: “you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). The new Israel needs its twelve foundations before the Spirit comes.

Peter states what an apostle must be: “one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us”. And then the heart of the matter: “one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.” An apostle is first of all a witness, someone who has walked with Jesus and seen him risen. Two names are proposed: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. Then the community prays: “Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen”. Notice the words: not whom we prefer, but whom you have chosen. They cast lots, an old way in Israel of leaving the decision to God (“The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the LORD’s alone,” Proverbs 16:33), and the lot falls on Matthias. It is the last time Scripture shows the Church choosing by lot; after Pentecost the Spirit will guide her through prayer, discernment and the laying on of hands. Joseph Justus, not chosen, disappears from the story without a word of complaint, a quiet lesson for every one of us who is passed over. Ancient tradition is uncertain about where Matthias later preached and died; Eusebius records the opinion that he had been one of the seventy disciples, and a tradition holds that his relics rest in Trier in Germany, where an abbey bears his name. We know little about him; we know the one thing that matters: he was chosen by the Lord to witness to the Resurrection.

The first reading for the feast explains how God chooses. Samuel comes to Bethlehem to anoint a king among the sons of Jesse. He sees Eliab, tall and impressive, and thinks, surely this is the one. “But the LORD said to Samuel, ‘Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for the LORD does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.’” Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. “Are all your sons here?” “There remains yet the youngest, but he is keeping the sheep.” The boy nobody thought to call is the one God has chosen; Samuel anoints him, “and the spirit of the LORD came mightily upon David from that day forward.” The pattern is clear: God looks on the heart, chooses the one who seems least, and then gives his Spirit. Paul writes the same truth to the proud Corinthians: “Consider your own call, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong”. Why? “so that no one might boast in the presence of God.” Our worth is not in our talents but in Christ, “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption”.

The Gospel lets us hear Jesus praying with joy: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants”. The fishermen of Galilee, the tax collector, the zealot, and now Matthias, were such infants: not learned men, but men to whom the Father had revealed the Son. Then comes the invitation that every apostle has carried to the ends of the earth: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart”. The apostolic office is not a crown but a yoke shared with Christ; bishops, priests and every baptised person who serves learn from the gentle and humble heart of Jesus or they do not learn at all. Our Syro-Malabar Church calls herself the Church of the Mar Thoma Christians, proud of her apostolic origin. Today's feast reminds us that apostolic faith rests not on our pride but on God's choice and on the witness to the Resurrection handed down from those first Twelve. The weekday readings echo the same call: “Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you” (1 John 2:24), and “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13). Matthias stayed with Jesus from the beginning, and endured to the end.
conn: Twelve thrones.
Jesus promised the Twelve that “you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28); the number must be complete before Pentecost.
Let another take his office.
Peter applies the psalm to Judas: “‘Let another take his position of overseer.’” (Acts 1:20).
I chose you.
“You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last” (John 15:16).
Taken from the sheepfolds.
“He chose his servant David, and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70); the youngest son, keeping the sheep, is anointed.
Witnesses chosen by God.

Peter later tells Cornelius that the Risen Lord appeared “not to all the people but to us who were chosen by God as witnesses, and who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
The Spirit after the anointing.
On David “the spirit of the LORD came mightily” after his anointing (1 Samuel 16:13); on Matthias and the eleven the Spirit will come at Pentecost (Acts 2:4).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana we pray in communion with the apostles, whose faith our Church received through Mar Thoma. The bishop who presides in our eparchy stands in the line of those Twelve, completed on this day by Matthias.
The Lord who chose the least of Jesse's sons and the unknown Matthias chooses us also to come to his altar; at Communion he says again, Come to me, and I will give you rest.
outline: Opening
An apostle known for one story only, chosen in the days of waiting with Mary.
Point 1 · The place must be filled
The Twelve and the twelve tribes; the wound of Judas healed by the praying Church.
Point 2 · A witness to his resurrection
Walking with Jesus from the beginning, and the lot that falls on Matthias.
Point 3 · The LORD looks on the heart
David the youngest, and the weak chosen to shame the strong.
Point 4 · Revealed to infants
The gentle yoke that every apostle carries.
Closing image
Joseph Justus, not chosen, going home in peace and still praying with the Church.
Take-home line
“Lord, you know everyone’s heart.”
live: Pray before choosing (Acts 1:24)
Before any decision today, at work or at home, pray: Lord, you know the heart; show me what you have chosen.
Do not look on appearance (1 Samuel 16:7)
Notice today someone usually overlooked, and give that person your time and respect.
Accept being passed over (Acts 1:23)
If you are not chosen, not thanked or not noticed today, offer it quietly like Joseph Justus.
Take his yoke (Matthew 11:29)
Bring one heavy burden to the Lord in prayer this evening and leave it with him.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Peter, as the first of the apostles, could have chosen alone, yet he acts with all the brethren, so that the choice may be beyond dispute. They pray, “You know the hearts”, for they wanted not their own choice but the Lord's; and they rightly place the decision in the hands of God, since the Spirit had not yet come.
St Clement of Rome (in substance)

The apostles received the Gospel from the Lord Jesus Christ, and Christ was sent from God. Having been filled with the Holy Spirit, they preached and appointed those who would succeed them, so that the ministry would continue in the Church in good order.
magis: Catechism 765

The Lord Jesus endowed his community with a structure: the choice of the Twelve with Peter as their head. Representing the twelve tribes of Israel, they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem.
Catechism 857
The Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, chosen witnesses sent out on mission by Christ himself.
Catechism 861
In order that the mission entrusted to them might be continued after their death, the apostles consigned to their immediate collaborators the duty of completing the work they had begun.
Catechism 489
Throughout the Old Covenant God prepared the mission of Mary; against all human expectation he chooses those considered powerless and weak to show his faithfulness.
Catechism 459
The Word became flesh to be our model of holiness: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.”
saints: Today
St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha), chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve (Acts 1:15–26). In the Latin calendar a feast on the same day (since 1969; formerly 24 February).
This week

14–16 May: the last days of the Season of the Resurrection. Fri 14: St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha), kept the same day in the Latin calendar. Sat 15: Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest, an important Marian feast; in the Latin Church the Vigil of Pentecost is celebrated in the evening. Sun 16: First Sunday of the Apostles, the Feast of Pentecost; the Season of the Apostles begins.
2027-05-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you chose the Twelve to be witnesses of your Resurrection, and when one place was left empty you filled it through the prayer of your Church gathered with your Mother. Through the prayers of Mar Mathias Shleeha and of Mar Thoma our father in faith, keep our Church faithful to the apostolic faith. You look on the heart and not on appearance: purify our hearts, teach us to accept your choices without envy, and give us your gentle and humble heart. As we wait with Mary for the Holy Spirit, make us witnesses of your Resurrection in our homes and our work. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-15.title: Seventh Saturday of Resurrection · Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest
2027-05-15.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You shall observe the festival of harvest
The threshing floors shall be full of grain; I will pour out my spirit
The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable
Not one of these little ones should be lost
2027-05-15.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. These are the days between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the Church, like the apostles with Mary in the upper room, prays for the coming of the Holy Spirit. The Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest, is listed in the First Set calendar as an important Marian feast, with the readings above (the NRSV has no verse 18:11 in Matthew). Weekday readings of the Seventh Saturday: 1 Corinthians 9:13–18; Matthew 18:23–35. This is the last day of the Season of the Resurrection: tomorrow is Pentecost. In the Latin Church the Vigil of Pentecost is celebrated this evening; the Syro-Malankara calendar also keeps today a commemoration of the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-05-15.verse: The threshing floors shall be full of grain, the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.
theo: On the last day of the Season of the Resurrection, on the eve of Pentecost, our Church turns to the Mother of God under a title that belongs to farmers and to the soil: the Protectress of Harvest. In the lands of Mesopotamia where the East Syriac tradition grew up, the middle of May is the time when the ears of grain ripen and the harvest is gathered; it is fitting to place our fields and our bread under the care of the Mother of the One who called himself the bread of life. The Syro-Malankara calendar keeps a similar commemoration today, of the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain. It is a feast of the earth, and it is also a feast of heaven, because the readings chosen for it lead us straight to the festival that Christians will celebrate tomorrow. The first reading is short: “Three times in the year you shall hold a festival for me.” The second of those festivals is “the festival of harvest, of the first fruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field.” This is the Feast of Weeks, counted seven weeks from the first sheaf, “fifty days” (Leviticus 23:16); in Greek it was called Pentecost, the fiftieth day. On that very festival, in Jerusalem, the Holy Spirit came down on the apostles gathered with Mary, and the first harvest of the Church was gathered in: “that day about three thousand persons were added” (Acts 2:41).

The prophet Joel speaks to a land that had been stripped by locusts and drought. Now God promises a reversal: “Do not fear, O soil; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things!” The pastures grow green, the fig tree and the vine bear again, the early and the later rain come in their season. “The threshing floors shall be full of grain, the vats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will repay you for the years that the swarming locust has eaten”. Every farmer in Kerala understands those words, in a month when the fields wait for the monsoon that usually arrives around the beginning of June, and many families still pray for the rain before sowing. But Joel goes further than the harvest: “Then afterward I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.” Tomorrow Peter will stand up in Jerusalem and say: “this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16). The rain on the fields becomes the sign of a greater rain, the Spirit poured out on men and women, young and old, servants and masters alike. Mary, the humble servant of the Lord, is the first to receive that rain in fullness: at the Annunciation the Holy Spirit came upon her, and in the upper room she prays with the apostles for the same Spirit to be poured upon the Church.

Paul's words to the Romans may seem far from the fields, but they speak of God's faithfulness to his first harvest, Israel. “A hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved”. Paul, himself a son of Israel, insists: “as regards election they are beloved, for the sake of their ancestors; for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” The Church has learned to read these words with great respect for the Jewish people, the people of the covenant never revoked, to whom belong the patriarchs, the prophets and, according to the flesh, Christ himself and his Mother. Mary is the daughter of Zion in whom the hope of Israel came to its fruit; Elizabeth greeted her: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). Paul ends with a word about all of us: “For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.” The harvest God desires is a harvest of mercy, in which no one is left in the field.

That is exactly what the Gospel says. “Take care that you do not despise one of these little ones; for, I tell you, in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven.” Then Jesus tells of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one that went astray, and rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine. “So it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.” The Protectress of Harvest is not only the guardian of rice and wheat; she is the Mother who watches over the little ones and the lost, as a farmer's wife watches over every sheaf. Mothers in Kerala homes know this: when one child is far away or has stopped praying, the rosary is said with that child's name. The weekday Gospel of the unforgiving servant adds a warning that fits a harvest feast: we who have received everything as a gift must forgive “from your heart” (Matthew 18:35), or the harvest is spoiled. And the weekday Epistle gives Paul's cry, “woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16): the Lord of the harvest needs labourers. So on this last evening of Easter we bring to Mary our fields and our work, our children near and far, and our hearts, asking her to prepare them, like good soil, for the rain of the Holy Spirit tomorrow.
conn: Fifty days.
“You shall count until the day after the seventh sabbath, fifty days; then you shall present an offering of new grain to the LORD” (Leviticus 23:16): the harvest festival is Pentecost.
Joel fulfilled.
Peter will say at Pentecost, “No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16).
The first harvest of the Church.
“So those who welcomed his message were baptized, and that day about three thousand persons were added” (Acts 2:41).
The land yields its increase.
“The LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase” (Psalm 85:12); the Fathers read such verses of the Incarnation, when the Virgin gave us Christ.
The grain of wheat.
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).
The Lord of the harvest.
“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we offer bread and wine, the fruit of the earth and of human work: the harvest of our fields becomes, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the Body and Blood of Christ, the true harvest born of the Virgin Mary.
Mary stood beside the altar of the Cross; she stands beside every altar where her Son offers himself. Today we place on the altar our fields, our labour and our children, through her hands.
outline: Opening
A Marian feast of the soil on the eve of Pentecost.
Point 1 · The festival of harvest
Fifty days, first fruits, and the first harvest of the Church.
Point 2 · I will pour out my spirit
Rain on the land, and the greater rain of the Spirit; Mary the first to receive it.
Point 3 · The gifts of God are irrevocable
Israel beloved; mercy on all.
Point 4 · Not one little one lost
The shepherd and the Mother who watch over the lost.
Closing image
A farmer's family in Kuttanad praying the rosary for rain before sowing, with one name added for a son far away.
Take-home line
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh.”
live: Bring your first fruits (Exodus 23:16)
Offer to God the first part of something you receive this week: your first hour, first earnings, or first fruit from your garden.
Pray for rain and for the Spirit (Joel 2:23, 28)
Pray today for farmers waiting for the monsoon, and ask Mary to prepare your heart for Pentecost.
Search for the one (Matthew 18:12)
Call or visit someone who has drifted from the family or from the Church.
Forgive from the heart (Matthew 18:35)
Before tomorrow's Pentecost Qurbana, forgive one person in your heart and, if you can, tell them.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)

The field that no one had sown brought forth the Sheaf of blessing; the earth that had not been ploughed gave us the Bread of life. Blessed is the Virgin, from whom came the Harvest that feeds the world.
St Augustine (in substance)

Fifty days after the Passover in Egypt, the Law was given on Sinai, written by the finger of God; fifty days after the Pasch of Christ, the Holy Spirit, the finger of God, came down, writing the law of love not on tablets of stone but on hearts.
magis: Catechism 731
On the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ's Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 969
Taken up to heaven, Mary did not lay aside her saving office, but by her manifold intercession continues to bring us the gifts of eternal salvation.
Catechism 1350
The offertory: we bring bread and wine to the altar, the gifts of the Creator in the hands of Christ.
Catechism 605
Jesus teaches that it is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should be lost; his love excludes no one.
Pope Francis, Laudato si’ 241
Mary, who cared for Jesus, now cares with maternal affection and pain for this wounded world; we can ask her to help us look at the world with wiser eyes.
saints: Today

Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest: in the First Set an important Marian feast, the last day of the Season of the Resurrection and the eve of Pentecost. Pray for farmers, fishermen and all who work the land and the sea.
This week

14–16 May: the last days of the Season of the Resurrection. Fri 14: St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha), kept the same day in the Latin calendar. Sat 15: Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest, an important Marian feast; in the Latin Church the Vigil of Pentecost is celebrated in the evening. Sun 16: First Sunday of the Apostles, the Feast of Pentecost; the Season of the Apostles begins.
2027-05-15.prayer: Holy Mother of God, Protectress of Harvest, you are the good soil from which came forth Christ, the Bread of life. We place under your care our fields and gardens, the rain and the seasons, the work of our hands, and the bread on our tables. Watch over the little ones and over all who have gone astray, that not one may be lost. On this eve of Pentecost, pray with us as you prayed with the apostles, that the Father may pour out his Spirit on our sons and daughters, on the old and the young, and that the harvest of mercy may be gathered in. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-05-17.title: First Monday of the Apostles · Mary, Mother of the Church
2027-05-17.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Let all things be done for building up
Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart
2027-05-17.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), the seven weeks that begin at Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari; from Pentecost “The Angel of the Lord” (the Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The First Set appendix lists Mary, Mother of the Church (Mater Ecclesiae) on the Monday after Pentecost, without proper readings: the readings of the day are used. In the Latin calendar it is an obligatory memorial (since 2018).
2027-05-17.verse: for God is a God not of disorder but of peace.
theo: On the day after Pentecost the Church looks at the woman who was in the upper room when the Spirit came. Luke had named her among the praying disciples: “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). At the Cross Jesus had given her to the beloved disciple with the words “Woman, here is your son,” and to the disciple, “Here is your mother” (John 19:26–27). The Church has always understood that in that disciple all disciples are given a Mother. On 21 November 1964, at the Second Vatican Council, St Paul VI solemnly proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church, that is, of the whole people of God, faithful and pastors. In 2018 Pope Francis placed this memorial on the Monday after Pentecost, so that the Church, newly born of the Spirit, might begin her journey with her Mother. Our First Set calendar lists the day without proper readings, and so we hear the readings of the first weekday of the Season of the Apostles; they speak, as it turns out, of the Church at prayer and of the humble heart, the two things Mary teaches best. She is not above the Church as a goddess, nor outside it as a spectator; she is its first and most perfect member, and for that very reason its Mother.

Paul writes to an assembly that has received many gifts of the Spirit and is in danger of turning them into noise. Everyone wants to speak at once. “When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.” Tongues only with interpretation, prophets one by one, the others weighing what is said, the first speaker silent when another receives a revelation: “For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged.” The reason is theological, not merely practical: “for God is a God not of disorder but of peace.” The Spirit who came at Pentecost with wind and fire is the same Spirit of order and peace. Our Syro-Malabar liturgy, with its fixed prayers, its roles for priest, deacon, choir and people, and its moments of silence, is a school in Paul's teaching: each voice in turn, everything for building up. Mary is the model of such a gift. She speaks little in the Gospels; she treasures and ponders (Luke 2:19). Her few words build up: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). In a Church tempted by noise and rivalry, the Mother of the Church teaches silence that listens and speech that serves.

The Gospel returns us to the prayer of Jesus: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants”. If anyone was such an infant before God, it was Mary, who sang that the Lord “has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant”. Jesus continues: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Where did the human heart of Jesus learn its gentleness? From the Father, first of all; and also in the home of Nazareth, from a mother who was gentle and humble. The Mother of the Church does not draw us to herself; she leads us to her Son, who gives rest to the weary. Many in our parishes carry heavy burdens: illness, debt, a broken marriage, children far away, loneliness in old age. On this first day of the Season of the Apostles, the Church, with Mary her Mother, says to them what her Son says: Come to him. Learn from him. His yoke is easy and his burden light, because he carries it with you.
outline: Opening
The woman in the upper room on the morning after Pentecost.
Point 1 · Here is your mother
From the Cross to the Council: Mary, Mother of the whole Church.
Point 2 · A God not of disorder but of peace
Gifts in turn, everything for building up; Mary's silence and her few words.
Point 3 · Learn from me, gentle and humble
The infant to whom the Father reveals, and rest for the weary.
Take-home line
“Here is your mother.”
live: Take her into your home (John 19:27)
Pray one decade of the rosary today with your family, entrusting your home to the Mother of the Church.
Build up, do not tear down (1 Corinthians 14:26)
Before you speak in a meeting or a family discussion today, ask: will this build up?
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

Mary is the type of the Church, in the order of faith, charity and perfect union with Christ. Like the Church she is virgin and mother: a virgin in her undivided faith, a mother who brings forth children for God.
St Augustine (in substance)

Mary is truly the mother of the members of Christ, because by her love she cooperated so that the faithful might be born in the Church, who are members of that Head of whom she is the mother according to the flesh.
magis: Catechism 963
The Virgin Mary is acknowledged as the true Mother of God and of the Redeemer; she is clearly the mother of the members of Christ. Mary, Mother of Christ, Mother of the Church.
Catechism 965
After her Son's Ascension, Mary aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers; in the upper room we see her prayerfully imploring the gift of the Spirit.
Catechism 801
Discernment of charisms is always necessary; no charism is exempt from being referred and submitted to the Church's shepherds, so that all may work together for the common good.
saints: Today

Mary, Mother of the Church (Mater Ecclesiae): listed in the First Set appendix for the Monday after Pentecost, without proper readings. Proclaimed by St Paul VI on 21 November 1964; inscribed in the General Roman Calendar as a memorial by Pope Francis in 2018.
2027-05-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, from the Cross you gave your Mother to the beloved disciple and to all your disciples. Grant that your Church, born of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, may grow in faith and love under the care of Mary, her Mother. Make our assemblies places of peace and not of disorder, where every gift builds up the body. Teach us, with her, to be little before the Father, and give us your gentle and humble heart, that the weary may find rest in you through us. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Mary stood by the Cross when the Sacrifice was offered; she stands, as Mother of the Church, by every altar where the Holy Qurbana makes that Sacrifice present. With her we offer and receive her Son.

2027-05-18.title: First Tuesday of the Apostles
2027-05-18.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Worthy of the kingdom for which you suffer
Lord, let our eyes be opened
2027-05-18.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), the seven weeks that begin at Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari; from Pentecost “The Angel of the Lord” (the Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. In the Latin calendar today: St John I, pope and martyr (optional memorial).
2027-05-18.verse: Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. Immediately they regained their sight and followed him.
theo: Jesus is leaving Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem, where the Cross awaits him. A large crowd follows him, and by the roadside sit two blind men. They cannot see him, but they hear that he is passing by, and they cry out: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” The crowd, perhaps embarrassed, perhaps impatient, tells them to be quiet. “But they shouted even more loudly, ‘Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David!’” Their prayer is short, repeated, and stubborn. It is the prayer the Church has never stopped praying: in our Holy Qurbana and in the Prayer of the Hours we say again and again, Lord, have mercy; the Christian East has made of it the Jesus Prayer, repeated with every breath. There is always a crowd that tells us to be quiet: the voice of shame, of busyness, of people who think prayer is useless. The blind men teach us to cry louder. And notice what happens next: “Jesus stood still.” The One who has set his face towards Jerusalem stops for two beggars. No one is too small to halt the Lord on his way.

“What do you want me to do for you?” Jesus knows what they need, yet he asks. He wants them to say it, to name their deepest desire. “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” Matthew gives the reason for what follows in one phrase: “Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes.” The word for compassion is the one Matthew uses when Jesus sees the crowds like sheep without a shepherd: a love that moves the depths of the heart. He does not heal from a distance; he touches. “Immediately they regained their sight and followed him.” They do not go home to enjoy their new sight; they follow him on the road that leads to Jerusalem, to the Cross and to the Resurrection. In this first week of the Season of the Apostles, the Gospel shows us what the apostles became: people whose eyes had been opened by Jesus and who followed him wherever he went. Isaiah had said that the Servant would come “to open the eyes that are blind” (Isaiah 42:7). Every Baptism, which the ancient Church called illumination, is such an opening of the eyes; every confession and every Qurbana can be another touch of the Lord's compassion.

Paul writes to the young Church of Thessalonica with a pastor's pride: “your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.” They are suffering persecution, and he does not hide it, but he sees their “steadfastness and faith during all your persecutions and the afflictions that you are enduring” as a sign that God is making them “worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering.” The strong language about God's judgment that follows is not a call to revenge; it is the assurance that God sees, that injustice will not have the last word, and that the Lord Jesus will be revealed “to be glorified by his saints and to be marveled at on that day among all who have believed.” Christians in many places, and in our own country, have known such afflictions; the faithful of Kandhamal in Odisha in 2008 are still remembered. Paul's answer to suffering is prayer: “To this end we always pray for you, asking that our God will make you worthy of his call and will fulfill by his power every good resolve and work of faith, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him”. Faith that grows, love that increases, steadfastness under trial, and a prayer for one another: this is the portrait of an apostolic Church.
outline: Opening
Two blind men by the road out of Jericho, and the crowd that says, Be quiet.
Point 1 · Lord, have mercy on us
The stubborn prayer, and the Lord who stands still.
Point 2 · What do you want me to do for you?
Compassion that touches, and eyes opened to follow.
Point 3 · Worthy of his call
Faith growing, love increasing, steadfast under trial.
Take-home line
“Lord, let our eyes be opened.”
live: Cry louder (Matthew 20:31)
Pray the Jesus Prayer slowly ten times today: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner.
Pray for the persecuted (2 Thessalonians 1:4)
Pray today for Christians who suffer for their faith in India and elsewhere, and for those who make them suffer.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The crowd that tried to silence the blind men is the noise of our bad habits and of those who mock the life of prayer. When Christ passes by, let us cry out all the more, and he will stand still and give us light.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See their gratitude: once their eyes were opened, they did not leave him but followed him. They had asked for nothing small, not money or bread, but sight; and having received it, they gave him back their whole life.
magis: Catechism 2616
Jesus hears the prayer of faith; the urgent request of the blind men, “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” has been renewed in the traditional prayer to Jesus known as the Jesus Prayer.
Catechism 1503
Christ's compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a resplendent sign that God has visited his people; he often touches those he heals.
Catechism 2667
The invocation of the holy name of Jesus, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners,” can be repeated in every circumstance and keeps us in the presence of God.
2027-05-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David, you stood still on the road for two blind beggars and opened their eyes with the touch of your compassion. Have mercy on us. Open the eyes of our hearts to see you, and let us follow you on the road you walk. Make our faith grow and our love for one another increase; keep steadfast all who suffer for your name, and make us worthy of your call, that your name may be glorified in us. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we pray, Lord, have mercy, like the blind men of Jericho. And the Lord stands still among us, touches us in his Body and Blood, and opens our eyes to recognise him and to follow him.

2027-05-19.title: First Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-05-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: When you come together to eat, wait for one another
The mustard seed and the yeast
2027-05-19.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), the seven weeks that begin at Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari; from Pentecost “The Angel of the Lord” (the Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives the Epistle as 1 Corinthians 11:31–34a. The Syro-Malankara calendar today recalls the tradition of the first offering of the Holy Qurbono by Mar Yaqob Shleeha.
2027-05-19.verse: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field;
theo: Three days after Pentecost, in the first week of the Season of the Apostles, the Gospel gives us two small parables about the growth of the Church. “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field; it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” Think of the beginning: about one hundred and twenty people in an upper room, a handful of fishermen, a few women, the Mother of Jesus. Think of what came of it: on the day of Pentecost three thousand, and within a few generations communities from Spain to Persia and, as our tradition holds, to the coast of Malabar. The image of the tree in whose branches the birds nest comes from the prophets. Ezekiel saw God plant a tender sprig on the mountain of Israel, so that it would become a noble cedar: “Under it every kind of bird will live” (Ezekiel 17:23). The birds are the nations. Our Church, which began, as tradition holds, with the preaching of Mar Thoma among a few families of Malabar, is one of those branches. That is not a reason for pride but for gratitude, and for patience: God's work begins small and grows slowly, and it is God who gives the growth.

The second parable is even more hidden. “The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.” Three measures of flour is a great quantity, enough bread for a large household; it is what Sarah prepared when the three visitors came to Abraham (Genesis 18:6). The yeast disappears into the dough; no one sees it working, yet nothing stays as it was. So the Gospel works in the world: not usually through spectacle, but through Christians mixed into ordinary life, in offices and fields, in hospitals and classrooms, in families, quietly changing everything from within. Matthew adds that Jesus spoke in parables to fulfil the prophecy: “I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.” What was hidden from the beginning is God's plan to gather all peoples into one, and Pentecost has revealed it. The apostles were the first yeast; today it is our turn to be mixed into the dough of our society without losing our flavour.

Paul's words to the Corinthians concern the Lord's Supper, and they come right after his account of its institution. Some in Corinth were eating their own meal before the poor arrived, so that “one goes hungry and another becomes drunk.” Paul warns: “But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged.” And he gives a simple rule: “So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.” Before we receive the Body of the Lord, we examine ourselves; our Church has always taught that one who is conscious of grave sin should first approach the sacrament of Reconciliation. And the Body we receive makes us one body with the poor, the late, the one who has nothing to bring. The mustard seed and the yeast grow in a community that waits for one another. It is fitting that the Syro-Malankara calendar recalls today the tradition of the first offering of the Holy Qurbono by Mar Yaqob Shleeha in Jerusalem: from that small first breaking of bread, the Eucharist of the apostles has spread like yeast through the whole world, and it reaches our altar every day.
outline: Opening
One hundred and twenty in an upper room, and the Church across the world.
Point 1 · The mustard seed
Small beginnings, the great tree and the birds of every nation.
Point 2 · The yeast in three measures of flour
Hidden, mixed in, changing everything from within.
Point 3 · Wait for one another
Examining ourselves, and the Eucharist that makes us one with the poor.
Take-home line
“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed.”
live: Do not despise small beginnings (Matthew 13:32)
Begin one small good thing today, a daily prayer, a visit, a saving for the poor, and trust God with its growth.
Wait for one another (1 Corinthians 11:33)
At the next family meal or parish gathering, make sure the last and least are served first.
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

Christ himself is the grain of mustard seed: small and despised in his Passion, but when crushed he poured out his power, and buried in the earth he rose as a tree whose branches shelter all who believe.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The leaven, though small, changes the whole lump when it is mixed in; so the apostles, twelve men, leavened the whole world. But the leaven must be mixed in, not kept apart: we must go among others and not lose our strength.
magis: Catechism 546
Jesus' invitation to enter his kingdom comes in the form of parables; through them he invites people to the feast of the kingdom and asks for a radical choice.
Catechism 1385

To respond to the invitation to Communion we must prepare ourselves; St Paul urges an examination of conscience, and anyone conscious of grave sin must receive the sacrament of Reconciliation before coming to Communion.
Catechism 1397
The Eucharist commits us to the poor; to receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren.
2027-05-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you compared the kingdom to a mustard seed and to a little yeast. Make your Church grow from small beginnings into a tree that shelters every nation, and make us yeast hidden in the dough of our society, changing it from within. Teach us to examine ourselves before we come to your table, and to wait for one another, especially for the poor and the last. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In every Holy Qurbana a little bread, a few grains of wheat, becomes the Body of Christ, and that small host feeds the whole Church. The mustard seed and the yeast are present on our altar.

2027-05-20.title: First Thursday of the Apostles
2027-05-20.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The new covenant inscribed in the heart
2027-05-20.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar marks today the anniversary of the inauguration of the first Syro-Malabar Bishops' Synod (1993).
2027-05-20.verse: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
theo: Four days after Pentecost the Letter to the Hebrews sets before us the promise that the Holy Spirit came to fulfil. The author quotes the prophet Jeremiah at length: “The days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” It will not be like the covenant made on the day God took his people “by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” What will be new? “I will put my laws in their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” At Sinai the commandments were written on tablets of stone and carried in the ark. They were holy and good, but they stood outside the human heart, and the heart could break them. The new covenant does not throw the law away; it carries it inside. That is exactly what happened in the upper room. The Spirit who came down as fire did not hand the apostles a new set of tablets; he became the law of love within them. The Catechism says it simply: the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ (CCC 1965–1966). And the last line of the promise is the sweetest: “I will remember their sins no more.” The covenant written on the heart begins with forgiveness.

We must read the author's words about the first covenant with care. When he says that God has “made the first one obsolete”, he is speaking of the sacrifices and the priesthood of the Tabernacle, now fulfilled in the one sacrifice of Christ. He is not saying that God has abandoned the people he first loved. The Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121), and Paul says that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Jeremiah's promise was first spoken to Israel, “the house of Israel and the house of Judah”, and we Gentiles have been welcomed into it as guests made children. This is why the Church reads the Old Testament every day with reverence, and why our Syro-Malabar liturgy, heir of the Church of the East, keeps so many prayers and psalms of the Jewish people. The Spirit who writes the law on our hearts writes in the same handwriting that once traced the commandments on stone.

The Gospel takes us into the Temple of Jerusalem at Passover. Jesus finds cattle, sheep and doves for sale and money changers at their tables. He makes a whip of cords, drives them out, overturns the tables and says, “Take these things out of here! Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!” The disciples remember the psalm: “Zeal for your house will consume me.” His anger is not contempt for the Temple; it is love for it. Jesus went up to the Temple as a child, prayed there, taught there, and called it his Father's house (CCC 583–584). When the leaders ask for a sign, he answers, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” They think of the stones that had been under construction for forty-six years, “But he was speaking of the temple of his body.” The evangelist adds a line that belongs to this season: “After he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this; and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.” Remembering is the work of the Spirit, who teaches us everything and reminds us of all that Jesus said (John 14:26). The Risen Body of Christ is now the true Temple, the place where God and humanity meet (CCC 586).

Two more truths follow from this Gospel. First, those who belong to Christ become part of that Temple: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Our parish churches, with the madbaha set apart and the altar at its heart, are signs of the living Church made of people; the cleansing of the Temple must therefore happen first in us, where greed, noise and bargaining with God can so easily set up their tables. Second, the Gospel ends quietly: many believed because of the signs, “But Jesus on his part would not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people… for he himself knew what was in everyone.” He knows what is in us, every hidden motive. That could frighten us, but Hebrews has already given the answer: the One who knows our hearts is the One who writes his law on them and remembers our sins no more. Today the calendar also recalls the inauguration in 1993 of the first Synod of Bishops of our Church, after the Syro-Malabar Church was raised to a Major Archiepiscopal Church. A synod is a ‘walking together’. Let us pray that our bishops, gathered in the Spirit, may keep the house of God a house of prayer, and that the whole Church may walk together under the law of love.
conn: The covenant on the heart.
Jeremiah first spoke the promise: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33); Hebrews quotes it in full.
A heart of flesh.
Ezekiel adds: “A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
Zeal for your house.
The disciples recall Psalm 69:9: “It is zeal for your house that has consumed me.”
The sign of the temple.
At the trial of Jesus false witnesses twisted his saying about the temple (Mark 14:58); John explains its true meaning: the temple of his body.
Living water from the temple.
Ezekiel saw water flowing from below the threshold of the temple (Ezekiel 47:1); from the side of the crucified Body flowed blood and water (John 19:34).
You are God's temple.
Paul: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Body that was destroyed and raised in three days is placed on our altar: the true Temple comes to dwell in us when we receive him.
The covenant written on the heart is renewed at every Qurbana in the Blood of the new covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins: the sins that God promised to remember no more.
outline: Opening
Stone tablets in an ark, and a law written on a living heart.
Point 1 · I will write it on their hearts
The new covenant and the grace of the Spirit.
Point 2 · Stop making my Father's house a marketplace
The zeal of love that cleanses.
Point 3 · The temple of his body
The Risen Christ the true Temple, and we his living stones.
Closing image
A grandmother in Pala who still sweeps the parish church each Saturday, saying, ‘It is his house.’
Take-home line
“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
live: Let the Spirit write (Hebrews 8:10)
Choose one commandment you keep only from outside, and ask the Holy Spirit to make it a law of love within you.
Clear one table (John 2:16)
Name one place where you bargain with God or let money rule your prayer, and overturn that table this week.
Honour God's house
Come to church a few minutes early this Sunday, in silence, and help keep it clean and prayerful.
Pray for our Synod
Pray today for the bishops of the Syro-Malabar Synod, that they may walk together in the Spirit.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Those who sold doves in the Temple are a figure of those in the Church who seek their own gain from holy things, for the dove is the sign of the Holy Spirit. Christ drives them out with a whip of cords, the cords of their own sins, and wants his house to be a house of prayer.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The new covenant is not written with ink or on tablets but on the heart: God himself is the teacher, and he does not need letters to instruct those whom the Spirit has taught. This is the greatness of the new covenant: forgiveness, and knowledge of God given to the least as to the greatest.
magis: Catechism 1965–1966
The New Law, or the Law of the Gospel, is the work of Christ; it is the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ, as Jeremiah promised.
Catechism 583–584
Jesus showed the deepest respect for the Temple; he drove the merchants out of it because of his zeal for his Father's house.
Catechism 586
Jesus identified himself with the Temple, presenting himself as God's definitive dwelling place among us; his Body is the true Temple.
Catechism 121
The Old Testament is an indispensable part of Sacred Scripture; the Old Covenant has never been revoked.
Catechism 797
The Holy Spirit is the soul of the Mystical Body; the Church is the temple of the Holy Spirit.

2027-05-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true Temple of God, you were destroyed on the Cross and raised up on the third day. Pour out your Holy Spirit upon us and write your law on our hearts, so that we may know you from the least to the greatest. Cleanse the temple of our lives of every greed and every bargain, and make our parishes houses of prayer. Bless the bishops of our Synod, that they may walk together in your Spirit and lead your people in love. You know what is in each of us: remember our sins no more, and make us your living temple, to the glory of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

2027-05-21.title: First Friday of the Apostles · The Friday of Gold
2027-05-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A lame man is healed by the apostles
The blind see and the lame walk
2027-05-21.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Friday of Gold, the first Friday after Pentecost, an ordinary feast of the Oriental tradition, recalls the healing of the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple (Acts 3), the first miracle worked by the apostles after the coming of the Spirit. The calendar notes that if only two readings are chosen, it is proper to read from the Acts of the Apostles. Longer forms in the calendar: 1 Corinthians 12:28–13:13; Luke 7:1–23.
2027-05-21.verse: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.”
theo: On the first Friday after Pentecost the Churches of the Syriac tradition keep a feast with a shining name: the Friday of Gold. It looks back to the first sign worked by the apostles after the Holy Spirit came upon them. Peter and John go up to the Temple “at the hour of prayer, at three o’clock in the afternoon”, the hour at which, only weeks before, Jesus had died on the Cross. At the gate called Beautiful lies a man “lame from birth”, carried there daily to beg. He asks for alms. “Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, ‘Look at us.’” Then comes the sentence that gives the day its name, as it is commonly explained: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.” The Church of the apostles is poor in gold and rich in the Name. Peter takes the man by the right hand, raises him, and “immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.” The man enters the Temple “walking and leaping and praising God.” The man lame from birth, more than forty years old (Acts 4:22), who had lain outside the gate, now goes in. Pentecost is not only a wind and tongues of fire; it is a hand stretched out to a beggar at the door.

Isaiah had seen this day from afar. To exiles worn out by grief he cried: “Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who are of a fearful heart, ‘Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God.’” And then: “the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy.” The prophet sees a desert blooming, waters breaking out in the wilderness, and a road through it called “the Holy Way”, on which “the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing.” In Acts 3 that prophecy walks into the Temple on healed feet. The lame man leaping at the Beautiful Gate is a living sign that the age of the Messiah has begun, and that the Holy Way now runs through the Church of the apostles. Every parish that welcomes the weak, the disabled, the forgotten, and helps them go in to the house of God is walking that road.

Peter then speaks to the crowd in Solomon’s Portico. He refuses all credit: “why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?” The healing is the work of “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our ancestors”, who “has glorified his servant Jesus.” Peter speaks as a son of Israel to his own people, and his words about the Passion are hard. But notice how he continues: “And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” He does not condemn; he calls to repentance and blessing: “Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out, so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord.” And he ends with the promise to Abraham: “in your descendants all the families of the earth shall be blessed”, adding that God sent his servant “first to you, to bless you.” The Church has always read these words without blaming the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Christ (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). It is our sins, the sins of all, that brought the Lord to the Cross, and it is to all of us that the times of refreshing are offered.

Why does the calendar join to this feast Paul's hymn to love? Because the healing at the gate was an act of love before it was an act of power. Paul has just listed the gifts of the Spirit, and now he says, “strive for the greater gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.” Without love, tongues are “a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal”; prophecy, knowledge and faith that moves mountains are nothing; even giving away all possessions gains nothing. “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude… It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends.” Peter had no gold, but he had this. He looked at the beggar, which the passers-by never did; he said, “Look at us”; he took him by the hand. The gold of this Friday is not the gold Peter lacked. It is love, which outlasts prophecies and tongues and knowledge: “And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.”

The Gospel shows us where the apostles learned this. At the gate of the town of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral: “He was his mother’s only son, and she was a widow.” Before any request is made, “When the Lord saw her, he had compassion for her and said to her, ‘Do not weep.’” He touches the bier, the bearers stand still, and he says, “Young man, I say to you, rise!” and “Jesus gave him to his mother.” When John the Baptist's disciples come to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?”, Jesus answers with Isaiah's own words: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them.” The gate of Nain and the Beautiful Gate belong together: what Jesus did at one gate, his apostles do at the other in his Name. In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns that she has no treasure of her own to give the world, only Christ, and that he is enough. The gold of our Church is not in her buildings or her accounts, but in the Name of Jesus spoken with love to someone lying at the door.
conn: The lame shall leap like a deer.
Isaiah 35:6 is fulfilled at the Beautiful Gate: the man enters “walking and leaping and praising God” (Acts 3:8).
Lift your drooping hands.
Hebrews takes up Isaiah 35:3: “Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees” (Hebrews 12:12).
No other name.
Before the council Peter explains the healing: “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).
The prophet like Moses.
Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15: “The Lord your God will raise up for you from your own people a prophet like me” (Acts 3:22).
The promise to Abraham.
“In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), recalled by Peter in Acts 3:25.
Another widow's son.
At Zarephath Elijah raised a widow's son and “gave him to his mother” (1 Kings 17:23); Luke uses the same words at Nain (Luke 7:15).
Signs of the Messiah.
Jesus' answer to John repeats Isaiah 35:5–6 and Isaiah 61:1: good news to the poor.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church, poor in silver and gold, gives what she has: the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, in whose Name the weak are made strong.
Peter and John went up to the Temple at the hour of prayer: the apostles' first sign came from the rhythm of prayer. From our Qurbana and our hours of prayer the strength comes to raise others up.
outline: Opening
A beggar at a beautiful gate, and two apostles with empty pockets.
Point 1 · Strengthen the weak hands
Isaiah's Holy Way and the lame who leap like a deer.
Point 2 · What I have I give you
The Name of Jesus, and a hand that raises up.
Point 3 · Repent, that times of refreshing may come
Peter's call to his own people, without blame and with blessing.
Point 4 · The more excellent way
Love that bears all things, the true gold of the Church.
Point 5 · Young man, rise
Compassion at the gate of Nain.
Closing image
A young volunteer in Thrissur pushing a wheelchair up the church steps for the Sunday Qurbana.
Take-home line
“What I have I give you.”
live: Look at the one at the gate (Acts 3:4)
Today, look into the eyes of one person you usually pass by, and speak to them.
Give what you have (Acts 3:6)
You may have no money to give; give time, a visit, a phone call, a prayer said with someone.
Make the way accessible (Isaiah 35:8)
Ask how your parish can help the disabled and elderly to come in: a ramp, a seat, someone to accompany them.
Read 1 Corinthians 13 slowly
Put your own name in place of ‘love’ and see where you fall short; ask the Spirit for that gift.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See the poverty of Peter and his wealth: he had no money, yet he gave what money cannot buy. Had he given silver, the man would soon have spent it and remained lame; he gave him his feet, and with his feet the praise of God.
St Augustine (in substance)

Love, and do what you will: if you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing but good can come.
magis: Catechism 1506–1507
Christ invites his disciples to follow him and share in his ministry of compassion and healing; the Risen Lord sends them, in his Name, to heal the sick.
Catechism 432
The name of Jesus signifies that the very name of God is present in the person of his Son; there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).
Catechism 597–598
The responsibility for the death of Jesus cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today; sinners were the authors of his Passion.
Catechism 1826
If I have not charity, says the Apostle, I am nothing; charity is superior to all the virtues, the first of the theological virtues.
Catechism 548–549
The signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him; by delivering some from hunger, sickness and death he announced a greater liberation, from sin.
saints: Today
The Friday of Gold, the first Friday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, St Christopher Magallanes, priest, and companions, martyrs of Mexico.
