16–22 May: first week of the Season of the Apostles. Mon 17: Mary, Mother of the Church. Thu 20: anniversary of the inauguration of the first Syro-Malabar Bishops' Synod (1993); in the Latin calendar, St Bernardine of Siena. Fri 21: the Friday of Gold; in the Latin calendar, St Christopher Magallanes and companions. Sat 22: in the Latin calendar, St Rita of Cascia. Sun 23: Second Sunday of the Apostles, the feast of the Most Holy Trinity; St Rita, listed for 23 May in the First Set, gives way to the feast (verify locally).
2027-05-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, at the gate of Nain you had compassion on a weeping mother, and at the Beautiful Gate your apostles raised the lame in your holy Name. Pour out on us the Holy Spirit who made them bold and gentle, so that we may look at those who lie at the door and give them what we have: your Name, our hands and our love. Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees; open the eyes of the blind and the hearts of the hard. Make your Church poor in gold and rich in charity, until all the ransomed of the Lord come to Zion with singing, and praise the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

2027-05-22.title: First Saturday of the Apostles
2027-05-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: We are one body in the Spirit
Believe in the one whom he has sent
2027-05-22.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Tomorrow, the Second Sunday of the Apostles, the Church keeps the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-22.verse: Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”
theo: The first week after Pentecost ends with Paul's great image of the Church: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.” Notice the last words. Paul does not say ‘so it is with the Church’, but “so it is with Christ.” The Church is not a club of people who admire Jesus; she is his Body, and he is her Head. At Pentecost the Spirit did not make the apostles a committee; he made them one living organism with the Risen Lord. Paul tells how this happened to each of us: in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, and we were all made to drink of one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). Baptism places us in the Body, Chrismation (Confirmation) gives us the Spirit to drink, and the Holy Qurbana, the one Bread, makes us one Body (1 Corinthians 10:17). The Catechism says that the unity of the body does not do away with the diversity of its members (CCC 791).

Then Paul turns playful, and his humour hides a sharp lesson. “If the foot would say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,’ that would not make it any less a part of the body.” He imagines an ear sulking because it is not an eye. “If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?” There are two temptations in a parish. One is envy: I am only a foot, so I am not needed; let the priest and the committee members do everything. The other is pride: I am the eye, and I see everything; the others are useless. Paul answers both with one sentence: “But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.” No one is in the Church by accident. The grandmother who prays the rosary at the back of the church, the altar server who rings the bell, the catechism teacher, the choir singer, the young man who carries chairs after the feast, the sick person offering pain at home: each is placed by God. In the Season of the Apostles, when we recall how the Church was born and sent, we are invited to ask not what the Church does for me, but where God has placed me in the Body.

The Gospel brings us to the morning after the multiplication of the loaves. The crowds have crossed the lake to find Jesus, and he sees through them: “you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.” Then he gives one of the great commands of John's Gospel: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you.” They ask the practical question: “What must we do to perform the works of God?” And Jesus answers: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” Faith is not idleness; it is the first and greatest work, the work that God himself does in us and with us. Everything else in the Christian life, our prayer, our service, our place in the Body, flows from believing in the One whom the Father sent. On Saturdays many of our families turn with love to the Blessed Virgin Mary, the first to believe the word of the angel and the Mother whom the apostles gathered around in the upper room (Acts 1:14). She is the model member of the Body: hidden, faithful, and wholly turned towards her Son. With her we learn to seek Jesus not for the bread he gives, but for himself, the Bread that endures for eternal life.
conn: One bread, one body.
“Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).
Many members in Christ.
Paul writes to Rome: “so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another” (Romans 12:5).
Saul, why do you persecute me?
At Damascus the Lord said to Saul, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:5): to strike the Body is to strike the Head.
The head of the body.
“He is the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18).
Bread that does not satisfy.
Isaiah asks, “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread?” (Isaiah 55:2).
Gathered with Mary.
After the Ascension the apostles devoted themselves to prayer “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the many members receive the one Body and become what they receive: the Body of Christ gathered around the one altar.
Jesus gives the food that endures for eternal life: the Bread we receive at the Qurbana is the Son of Man himself, on whom the Father has set his seal.
outline: Opening
A body in which the foot complains and the ear sulks.
Point 1 · So it is with Christ
The Church, his Body, born of the Spirit.
Point 2 · As God arranged, as he chose
No one in the Body by accident.
Point 3 · This is the work of God: believe
The food that endures, and the faith of Mary.
Closing image
A parish feast in Kuttanad where the youngest boy proudly folds the chairs while the elders sing the Lord's praises.
Take-home line
“This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”
live: Find your place (1 Corinthians 12:18)
Ask your parish priest or a council member where help is needed, and offer one hour this month.
Honour the hidden members
Thank one person in your parish whose service no one notices.
Work for the bread that endures (John 6:27)
Before your next meal, pray: Lord, give me also the bread that endures for eternal life.
Pray with Mary
On this Saturday pray a decade of the rosary for the unity of the Church.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
If you are the body of Christ and his members, it is your own mystery that is placed on the Lord's table; it is your own mystery that you receive. Be what you see, and receive what you are.
St Augustine (in substance)
Why do you prepare your teeth and your stomach? Believe, and you have eaten. To believe in him whom the Father sent is to eat the living Bread.
magis: Catechism 790–791
Believers who respond to God's word become members of Christ's Body; the unity of the body does not do away with the diversity of its members.
Catechism 1396
The unity of the Mystical Body: the Eucharist makes the Church.
Catechism 161–162
Believing in Jesus Christ and in the One who sent him is necessary for salvation; faith is a gift of God that we must nourish and persevere in.
Catechism 965
After her Son's Ascension, Mary aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers; she was present in the upper room praying for the gift of the Spirit.
saints: Today
First Saturday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, St Rita of Cascia, religious. The First Set lists St Rita on 23 May, where she gives way to the Trinity this year.
This week

16–22 May: first week of the Season of the Apostles. Mon 17: Mary, Mother of the Church. Thu 20: anniversary of the inauguration of the first Syro-Malabar Bishops' Synod (1993); in the Latin calendar, St Bernardine of Siena. Fri 21: the Friday of Gold; in the Latin calendar, St Christopher Magallanes and companions. Sat 22: in the Latin calendar, St Rita of Cascia. Sun 23: Second Sunday of the Apostles, the feast of the Most Holy Trinity; St Rita, listed for 23 May in the First Set, gives way to the feast (verify locally).
2027-05-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Head of the Church, by the one Spirit you baptized us into one Body and gave us one Spirit to drink. Forgive us when we envy the gifts of others or despise our own place; help each of us to serve where the Father has placed us. Give us hunger for the food that endures for eternal life, and the faith that is the work of God. With the Blessed Virgin Mary, who prayed with the apostles in the upper room, may we seek you for yourself and remain one in you, to the glory of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

2027-05-24.title: Second Monday of the Apostles
2027-05-24.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Hold true to what you have attained
Jesus, the Resurrection and the Life
2027-05-24.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The second week of the Season of the Apostles begins, the day after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-24.verse: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,”
theo: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison, and he writes as a father: “Only let us hold fast to what we have attained. Brothers and sisters, join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us.” It may sound bold to say ‘imitate me’, but Paul has just told them that he himself is still running, pressing on towards the goal (Philippians 3:12–14). He does not offer himself as a finished saint, but as a runner who has not stopped. Faith is passed on this way, from life to life. Every one of us learned to pray from someone: a mother at the evening prayer, a grandfather with his rosary, a catechism teacher, a priest. The Season of the Apostles reminds us that the Church was built on witnesses whose lives could be copied. The question for us is simple: if someone younger imitated my faith, would they come closer to Christ?

Then Paul's voice breaks: “For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears.” He describes them without hatred, with grief: “Their end is destruction; their god is the belly; and their glory is in their shame; their minds are set on earthly things.” These seem to be not pagans far away but baptized people who have made comfort and appetite their god. The danger is close to every one of us. Against it Paul sets one of the most beautiful lines of the New Testament: “But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.” Philippi was a Roman colony, proud of its citizenship; Paul tells them they belong to a greater city. And the Saviour we await “will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” Our bodies, weak and ageing, are not prisons to escape but seeds of the resurrection. The Catechism quotes these words when it teaches how we will rise: Christ will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (CCC 999).

The Gospel shows that hope at the graveside. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha goes out to meet Jesus and speaks with the honesty of grief: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.” Jesus says, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha answers with the faith of a devout Jewish woman of her time: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.” And Jesus brings the last day into the present: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” Resurrection is not only an event at the end; it is a Person standing before her. Martha's answer is one of the great confessions of the Gospel: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” In the Season of the Apostles, when the Church goes out to proclaim the Risen Lord, Martha teaches us the heart of that proclamation. Every Christian funeral in our parishes, with its prayers and its incense and its candles, repeats her words. And every time we visit a grieving family, we bring the same Lord to the door, asking quietly: “Do you believe this?”
conn: Pressing on.
Just before today's passage Paul says, “I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14).
Citizens of heaven.
Hebrews says of the patriarchs that “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).
The glorious body.
Paul to Corinth: “It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44).
I will open your graves.
Ezekiel 37:12: “I am going to open your graves, and bring you up from your graves, O my people.”
Martha's confession and Peter's.
Peter confesses, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16); Martha says the same at Bethany (John 11:27).
Martha who served.
In Luke 10:38–42 Martha is busy serving; here she is the first to run out to meet Jesus.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we receive the Body of the One who is the Resurrection and the Life: he gives us the pledge that our lowly bodies will be made like his glorious body.
The Qurbana is the meeting point of our two citizenships: on earth we gather at the altar, and the altar opens onto heaven, where our citizenship is.
outline: Opening
A letter from prison, and a father who writes with tears.
Point 1 · Join in imitating me
Faith passed on from life to life.
Point 2 · Our citizenship is in heaven
Enemies of the Cross, and the body of glory.
Point 3 · I am the resurrection and the life
Martha's grief and Martha's faith.
Closing image
A widow in Kottayam lighting the lamp on her husband's grave on his anniversary and praying, ‘Lord, I believe.’
Take-home line
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
live: Be someone worth imitating (Philippians 3:17)
Choose one young person who watches you, and let them see you pray this week.
Pray for those who have lost faith (Philippians 3:18)
Name one person who has drifted from the Church and pray for them with Paul's tears.
Remember your citizenship (Philippians 3:20)
Before you make a purchase or a choice this week, ask: does this suit a citizen of heaven?
Visit a grieving family (John 11:20)
Go, like Martha, to meet the Lord in a house of mourning: visit or call someone who has lost a loved one.
fathers: The Letter to Diognetus (in substance)

Christians live in their own countries, but as sojourners; they share in everything as citizens and endure everything as strangers. Every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland a foreign land. They pass their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven.
St Augustine (in substance)

Martha said, I know that he will rise on the last day. The Lord answered, I am the resurrection: as if to say, you speak of a day that is far off; but the One who will raise him then is here now, and whoever believes in him already passes from death to life.
magis: Catechism 994
Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: I am the resurrection and the life.
Catechism 999
How do the dead rise? Christ is raised with his own body; he will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).
Catechism 1002–1003
Christ will raise us up on the last day, but it is also true that in a certain way we have already risen with Christ through Baptism.
Catechism 2796
The Father's house is our homeland; we are citizens of heaven, while we are still on our way.

2027-05-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the resurrection and the life. At Bethany you met Martha in her grief and drew from her the confession of faith; meet us also in our sorrows, and make us say with her, Yes, Lord, I believe. Keep us from making our belly our god and setting our minds on earthly things. Remind us that our citizenship is in heaven, and teach us to live so that others may imitate us and come to you. 2027-05-25.title: Second Tuesday of the Apostles
2027-05-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You have the words of eternal life
2027-05-25.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. On Thursday our Church keeps the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ; today's Gospel closes the discourse on the Bread of Life.
2027-05-25.verse: Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
theo: Paul's letter to Corinth takes an unusual turn. Some in the community are questioning his authority, and he answers with a burst of questions: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?” His credentials are not a diploma but an encounter and a community: he has seen the Risen Lord, and the Corinthians themselves are “the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.” In the Season of the Apostles this matters to us. An apostle is one who has been sent by the Risen Christ, and the proof of the sending is the life of the Church that grows from it. Our own Church in Kerala is the seal of the apostleship of Mar Thoma, and every parish, every family that prays, every child who is baptized, is still that seal. Paul then defends a right: those who preach the Gospel may live by it. A soldier does not pay his own expenses, the one who plants a vineyard eats its fruit, the shepherd drinks the milk of the flock; and the Law says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” The Church has always taught that the faithful must help provide for the needs of the Church and of her ministers (CCC 2043).

Then comes the surprise. Having proved his right, Paul refuses to use it: “Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.” He worked with his own hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) so that no one could say he preached for money. Here is a principle for every Christian and every minister: what we are entitled to is not always what serves the Gospel. A priest may have a right to comfort, a parish committee to recognition, a parent to an apology, a worker to a holiday, and all may be just. But love sometimes lays a right aside so that Christ may be seen more clearly. The priests and religious who serve in our mission dioceses in North India, often in poverty and far from home, live this word of Paul every day. So do the parents who give up their own plans for a child with special needs. The question Paul puts to us is not ‘What am I owed?’ but ‘What might stand in the way of the Gospel, and can I remove it?’

The Gospel brings the long discourse on the Bread of Life to its crisis. Jesus has said, “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life” (John 6:54), and many disciples find it too hard. “Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.” Jesus does not run after them to soften his words; he does not explain the Eucharist away as a mere symbol. Instead he turns to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” And Simon Peter answers for them all: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life. We have come to believe and know that you are the Holy One of God.” Peter does not say that he understands everything. He says that there is no one else to go to. That is often the faith of the Church in hard times: not a clever answer to every question, but a loyal heart that knows where life is found. The Catechism places this very scene at the heart of its teaching on the Eucharist: the Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks, and the Lord's question echoes through the ages, inviting us to discover that only he has the words of eternal life (CCC 1336). The Gospel ends with a shadow: “Did I not choose you, the twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.” Even among the chosen, betrayal is possible. Two days before the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, let us renew our faith in the Real Presence, and pray for those who have walked away, that they may hear again the question of Jesus and come back.
conn: Fire in the bones.

Jeremiah could not stop speaking the word: “within me there is something like a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9); Paul: “woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16).
The ox that treads the grain.
Deuteronomy 25:4, quoted again in 1 Timothy 5:18: “The laborer deserves to be paid.”
Paul the tentmaker.
At Corinth Paul stayed and worked with Aquila and Priscilla, because they shared the same trade: they were tentmakers (Acts 18:3).
Peter's other confession.
At Caesarea Philippi Peter says, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16).
Whom have I but you?
The psalmist: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire other than you” (Psalm 73:25).
The Holy One of God.
Even an unclean spirit cried out, “I know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24); Peter confesses it in faith.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we stand where the Twelve stood: before the mystery of the Body and Blood of Christ that many found too hard. With Peter we say, Lord, to whom can we go? and receive the Bread of eternal life.
Paul laid aside his rights for the Gospel; at the altar Christ laid aside his glory and gave his very self. Every Communion invites us to give ourselves in the same way.
outline: Opening
A man who had every right, and gave it up.
Point 1 · Am I not an apostle?
The encounter with the Risen Lord and the seal of a living community.
Point 2 · No obstacle to the gospel
Rights laid aside for love.
Point 3 · Lord, to whom can we go?
The hard saying, the departing crowd, and Peter's loyal faith.
Closing image
A missionary sister from Kerala in a village of Madhya Pradesh, walking two hours to teach catechism, carrying nothing but a Bible and a water bottle.
Take-home line
“You have the words of eternal life.”
live: Support those who preach (1 Corinthians 9:11)
Give generously this month to your parish and to the missions of our Church.
Lay aside one right (1 Corinthians 9:12)
Give up one thing you are entitled to this week for the sake of peace or the Gospel.
Stay with Jesus (John 6:68)
When a teaching of the Church is hard for you, say Peter's prayer: Lord, to whom can I go? and ask for light.
Prepare for Thursday
Make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament before the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Peter answered for all, one for many, unity for the whole. Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life: as if to say, if we leave you, you who give us eternal life in your body and blood, where else shall we find it?
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

See how Paul, after proving his right, says he did not use it: he wants to show that he did more than the law required. He bore hunger and labour rather than give anyone a pretext to slander the Gospel.
magis: Catechism 1336

The first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples; the Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks; the Lord's question, Will you also go away?, invites us to discover that only he has the words of eternal life.
Catechism 1374

In the most blessed sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained.
Catechism 2043
The faithful have the duty of providing for the material needs of the Church, each according to his abilities.
Catechism 162
Faith is a gift of God; we can lose it; to live, grow and persevere in faith we must nourish it with the word of God and beg the Lord to increase it.

Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, kept by our Church on the Thursday (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Then Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles; Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2027-05-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Holy One of God, you have the words of eternal life. When your teaching is hard and many turn away, keep us with you, and give us the loyal faith of Peter, who knew there was no one else to go to. Teach us, like your apostle Paul, to lay aside our rights rather than put an obstacle in the way of your Gospel, and to support generously those who proclaim it. Bless the missionaries of our Church who labour far from home. As we prepare for the feast of your Body and Blood, deepen our faith in your true presence, and bring back to your table all who have walked away. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

2027-05-26.title: Second Wednesday of the Apostles
2027-05-26.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit
Anyone who comes to me I will never drive away
2027-05-26.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. In the Latin calendar today is the memorial of St Philip Neri.
2027-05-26.verse: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away;
theo: This week the Gospel takes us back to the synagogue at Capernaum and to the long discourse on the bread of life in the sixth chapter of John. Over the coming days we will hear it piece by piece, and on Thursday, the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ, we will hear its heart. Today Jesus speaks of those who come to him: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away.” The promise is unconditional. There is no person so wounded, so sinful or so unimportant that Jesus would push them back from his door. He explains why: “for I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” The Father's will is not a cold law; it is the will of a Father who does not want to lose a single child. Then come the murmurs: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How can he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?” The difficulty is familiarity. They know the carpenter's family, and so they cannot see the One who came from the Father. The evangelist uses the same word that the Bible uses for Israel's grumbling in the wilderness over the manna; these listeners, like the disciples a little later in the same chapter (John 6:60), stand where every believer sometimes stands, finding the words of Jesus hard. The danger is the same for us. We have known Jesus since our baptism, since the catechism class and the Sunday Qurbana of our childhood, and familiarity can hide him.

Jesus answers the grumbling with a word about grace: “No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me; and I will raise that person up on the last day.” Faith begins not with our cleverness but with the Father's drawing. That is good news for parents who pray for children who have drifted away, and for anyone who feels that faith is beyond them. The Father is already drawing; our part is not to resist. Four times in this chapter Jesus repeats the promise, “I will raise them up on the last day” (John 6:39, 40, 44, 54). The bread of life is not only for this life. It is a pledge of the resurrection of the body.

Paul's letter speaks of that same body. In Corinth some believers had a slogan: “All things are lawful for me.” Paul quotes it and corrects it twice: “but not all things are beneficial” and “but I will not be dominated by anything.” Christian liberty is not the right to be enslaved by appetite. The Corinthians thought that what one did with the body did not matter, since the body would perish anyway. Paul answers: “The body is meant not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And God raised the Lord and will also raise us by his power.” Because the body will rise, the body matters now. Then comes one of the great sentences of the New Testament: “Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.” Ten days ago, at Pentecost, we celebrated the coming of the Spirit on the apostles. In this Season of the Apostles Paul reminds us where the Spirit lives: in our bodies. That changes how we eat and drink, how we use our eyes on a screen at midnight, how we treat our own bodies and the bodies of others, how we care for the sick and the old, and how we lay our dead to rest. A temple is not something one abuses, rents out or neglects. It is something one keeps clean and fills with praise.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I believe that Jesus will never drive me away?
Point 1 · I will never drive away
The Father's will to lose no one; the murmurs of familiarity.
Point 2 · Drawn by the Father
Faith as a gift, and the promise of the last day.
Point 3 · A temple of the Holy Spirit
Bought with a price: glorify God in your body.
Take-home line
“You are not your own.”
live: Come without fear (John 6:37)
If you have stayed away from the sacrament of Reconciliation, go this week: the Lord does not drive away anyone who comes.
Glorify God in your body (1 Corinthians 6:20)
Choose one concrete discipline this week for the sake of the temple: no screen after a fixed hour, no drink, or a daily walk with a prayer.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

You are drawn not only by the will but by delight. Show a green branch to a sheep and you draw it; show nuts to a child and he runs to them. If earthly delights draw people, will not Christ draw us when the Father reveals him?
St Irenaeus of Lyons (in substance)

How can anyone say that the flesh is incapable of the gift of God, which is eternal life, when it is nourished by the Body and Blood of the Lord and is made a member of him? As the wheat falls into the earth and rises multiplied, so our bodies, fed by the Eucharist, will rise in their time.
magis: Catechism 364

The human body shares in the dignity of the image of God; it is a human body precisely because it is animated by a spiritual soul, and it is destined to become, in the Body of Christ, a temple of the Spirit.
Catechism 1004
In expectation of the last day, the believer's body and soul already share in the dignity of belonging to Christ; this demands reverence for one's own body and for the bodies of others.
Catechism 2337
Chastity means the successful integration of sexuality within the person, and so the inner unity of the human being in body and spirit.
saints: Today
Latin calendar: St Philip Neri (1515–1595), priest, the apostle of Rome, founder of the Congregation of the Oratory, remembered for his joy, his humour and his long hours in the confessional.
This week

26–31 May: second and third weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which closes the month of Mary. The Sacred Heart of Jesus falls on Friday 4 June.
2027-05-26.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came down from heaven to do the will of the Father, who wills that none of those he gives you should be lost. You never drive away anyone who comes to you. Draw us, and those we love who have wandered, into your company. Holy Spirit, you dwell in our bodies as in a temple: keep them pure and strong, make them instruments of praise and service, and raise them up with Christ on the last day. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who will raise us on the last day gives his own Body to our bodies. We receive him into the temple of the Spirit, and we go out bought with a price, to glorify God in the body he has fed.

2027-05-27.title: Second Thursday of the Apostles: the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ
2027-05-27.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Melchizedek brings out bread and wine
A pure offering in every place
This is my body that is for you
My flesh is true food and my blood is true drink
2027-05-27.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ is a Feast of Our Lord; the Syro-Malabar Church keeps it on the Thursday after the Feast of the Holy Trinity. The calendar notes the fuller passages: Genesis 14:1–20; Malachi 1:6–12; 1 Corinthians 10:15–17 with 11:23–30; John 6:51–64. In India the Latin Church keeps the solemnity of Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May (verify locally for parish processions and adoration).
2027-05-27.verse: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
theo: Two months after Easter, and eleven days after Pentecost, the Church stops on a Thursday to adore the gift that Jesus left on another Thursday, the night before he died. On Maundy Thursday the joy of the gift was overshadowed by the betrayal and the Passion. Today, in the Season of the Apostles, the Church celebrates the same gift in full light: the Body and Blood of Christ, given in every Holy Qurbana from the Upper Room to our own parish altar. The apostles, filled with the Spirit, did not only preach; they broke bread. The first believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). The Church that the apostles founded has been a Eucharistic Church from the first day. Our own Mar Thoma Christians received this faith from the apostle Thomas, and the word we use for the Eucharist, Qurbana, a Syriac word for offering or sacrifice, says what it is: the offering of Christ himself.

The first reading takes us back almost two thousand years before Christ. Abram returns from battle, having rescued his nephew Lot, and a mysterious figure comes out to meet him: “And King Melchizedek of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High.” He blesses Abram: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!” Melchizedek appears and disappears in three verses, yet the Bible never forgets him. The psalm says of the coming Messiah: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), and the Letter to the Hebrews sees in him an image of Christ, “resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever” (Hebrews 7:3). A king of peace and righteousness, a priest who offers bread and wine: the Church has always seen here the first outline of the Eucharist. At the altar our priest still offers bread and wine, and they become the Body and Blood of the eternal High Priest.

The second reading is a hard word to priests. Through the prophet Malachi God complains that the priests of the restored Temple are offering blind, lame and sick animals, the leftovers of the flock: “By offering polluted food on my altar. And you say, ‘How have we polluted it?’ By thinking that the Lord’s table may be despised.” God would rather the Temple doors were shut than that worship should continue carelessly. Then comes a promise that reaches far beyond Jerusalem: “For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts.” From the earliest centuries Christians read this verse as a prophecy of the Eucharist. The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, applies it to the Sunday breaking of bread, and St Justin and St Irenaeus did the same. Today, at every hour, somewhere from the rising of the sun to its setting, the Holy Qurbana is being offered, in Kerala and in Chicago, in Rome and in a forest chapel in Arunachal: one pure offering, Christ himself. Malachi's warning remains for us too. We can despise the Lord's table by arriving late and leaving early, by careless dress and wandering eyes, by giving God the leftovers of our Sunday.

In the Epistle Paul hands on the oldest written account of the Last Supper, written about twenty-five years after the event: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’” Received and handed on: this is what tradition means. Paul did not invent the Eucharist; he passed on what the Church already did. And he draws a serious conclusion: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord. Examine yourselves, and only then eat of the bread and drink of the cup.” The Corinthians were sharing the Lord's Supper while the rich ate well and the poor went hungry. To fail to discern the Body, Paul says, is to fail to see both Christ truly present in the sacrament and Christ present in the brothers and sisters gathered around it. That is why the Church asks us to confess serious sins before receiving, to keep the Eucharistic fast, and to come to Communion reconciled with our neighbour.

The Gospel is the heart of the discourse in Capernaum: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.” His hearers dispute: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” Jesus does not soften his words. He makes them stronger: “Very truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day; for my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink.” True food, true drink: not a symbol only, not a pious memory, but the real Christ. This is what the Catholic Church believes and what the Council of Trent called transubstantiation: at the consecration the whole substance of the bread becomes the Body of Christ and the whole substance of the wine his Blood, while the appearances remain. And the purpose of it all is communion: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.” Whoever receives the Lord worthily carries him out into the street, the office, the kitchen and the hospital ward. Many of our parishes will carry the Blessed Sacrament in procession in these days, under the umbrellas and through the lanes, with children scattering petals. It is the same mystery: Christ who comes to us in the Qurbana wants to go with us wherever we live.
conn: Bread and wine of Melchizedek.
“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4); Jesus has entered the sanctuary as “a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 6:20).
The pure offering.
Malachi 1:11 is applied to the Eucharist in the Didache (chapter 14) and by St Justin and St Irenaeus; the Church sees it fulfilled when Christ offers himself through the priest in every place.
The manna.
“It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat” (Exodus 16:15); “Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died” (John 6:49).
The Last Supper.
“Take; this is my body.” “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:22, 24).
Emmaus.
“He took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (Luke 24:30–31).
One bread, one body.
“The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17).
The cup of salvation.
“I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord” (Psalm 116:13).
altar: At the consecration the priest repeats the words of the Lord, “This is my body… this is my blood”, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, whom we invoke in the epiclesis of our anaphora, the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ. What Melchizedek foreshadowed and Malachi foretold is placed on our altar.

When we receive Holy Communion, the Lord says to each one what he said in Capernaum: whoever eats me will live because of me. Let us receive him with a clean heart, and carry him out of the church into our homes and streets.
outline: Opening
From the Upper Room to our parish altar: a Thursday of thanksgiving in the Season of the Apostles.
Point 1 · Bread and wine of Melchizedek
The priest-king who prefigures Christ.
Point 2 · A pure offering in every place
Malachi's warning and Malachi's promise.
Point 3 · Received and handed on
The words of institution and the call to examine ourselves.
Point 4 · True food and true drink
The Real Presence and abiding in Christ.
Closing image
A Eucharistic procession through the lanes of a Kerala parish, children scattering petals before the monstrance.
Take-home line
“Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.”
live: Discern the Body (1 Corinthians 11:29)
Before your next Communion, examine your conscience; if there is serious sin, go first to confession.
Do not despise the Lord's table (Malachi 1:7)
Come early to the Qurbana this Sunday, dress with reverence, and stay to the end and for a moment of thanks.
Abide in him (John 6:56)
Spend fifteen minutes this week before the Blessed Sacrament, in adoration or in a visit to the church.
Carry him to others
Take part in a Eucharistic procession or adoration in your parish, and bring a child or an elderly person with you.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian (in substance)
In your bread is hidden the Spirit who is not consumed; in your wine dwells the fire that is not drunk. The Spirit in your bread, the fire in your wine: a wonder heard from our own lips.
St Cyril of Jerusalem (in substance)

Do not regard the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ, as the Lord himself declared. Even if the senses suggest otherwise, let faith make you firm. Do not judge by taste, but be fully assured by faith.
St Justin Martyr (in substance)

We do not receive these as common bread and common drink. As Jesus Christ our Saviour was made flesh by the Word of God, so we have been taught that the food over which thanks has been given by his word is the flesh and blood of that same Jesus who was made flesh.
magis: Catechism 1333

At the heart of the Eucharistic celebration are the bread and wine that become the Body and Blood of Christ; the Church sees in the gesture of Melchizedek, who brought out bread and wine, a prefiguring of her own offering.
Catechism 1330
The Eucharist is called the Holy Sacrifice because it makes present the one sacrifice of Christ; it is also called the pure and holy sacrifice.
Catechism 1374
In the most blessed sacrament the Body and Blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained.
Catechism 1376

The Council of Trent: by the consecration the whole substance of bread is changed into the substance of the Body of Christ and the whole substance of wine into the substance of his Blood; this change the Church has fittingly called transubstantiation.
Catechism 1385
To respond to this invitation we must prepare ourselves; anyone conscious of a grave sin must receive the sacrament of Reconciliation before coming to Communion (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
St John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia 1
The Church draws her life from the Eucharist.
saints: Today
The Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Syro-Malabar calendar. In the Latin calendar, St Augustine of Canterbury; the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May.
This week

26–31 May: second and third weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. 2027-05-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, eternal High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, on the night you were betrayed you took bread and wine and gave us your Body and Blood. We adore you truly present in the Holy Qurbana, offered from the rising of the sun to its setting. Give us hearts that discern your Body, in the sacrament and in our brothers and sisters. Let us never despise your table, but come to it cleansed and grateful. Feed us with the living bread, that we may abide in you and you in us, and raise us up on the last day. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.

2027-05-28.title: Second Friday of the Apostles
2027-05-28.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God
I am the bread of life
2027-05-28.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven.
2027-05-28.verse: Very truly, I tell you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life.
theo: Yesterday we celebrated the Body and Blood of Christ; today the Gospel takes a step back in the same discourse at Capernaum and shows us the road that leads to the altar. Jesus quotes the prophets: “It is written in the prophets, ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.” The words come from Isaiah's promise to the restored Jerusalem, “All your children shall be taught by the Lord” (Isaiah 54:13). Before anyone eats the bread of life, they must first listen and learn. That is why every Holy Qurbana has two tables: first the table of the Word, with the readings and the homily, and then the table of the Body and Blood. Jesus adds at once that this learning is not mere information: “Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” Only the Son has seen the Father face to face. To be taught by God is to be taught by the Son, who makes the Father known.

Then comes the simple, tremendous claim: “Very truly, I tell you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life.” Jesus contrasts himself with the gift Israel remembered with gratitude: “Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.” The manna was a true gift of God; it kept a whole people alive for forty years in the desert. But it fed bodies that would one day die. The bread that Jesus gives, which is himself, feeds a life that death cannot end. Notice that faith comes before eating in this passage: whoever believes has eternal life. The Eucharist is truly Christ whatever our state, but it bears fruit only in a heart that believes. We come to the altar as people who have listened, learned and believed, and the Lord who is received into a believing heart gives life that lasts.

Paul's words to the Corinthians sound at first like an insult: “If you think that you are wise in this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” The Corinthians were proud of their learning and had divided into parties: some for Paul, some for Apollos, some for Cephas. Paul says that boasting about human leaders is foolish, and then he turns the whole question upside down: “For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future, all belong to you, and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.” The apostles do not own the Church; they serve it. The believer does not belong to a party, a preacher or a movement, but to Christ. In our own day the temptation is the same. We can make idols of favourite preachers, of retreat centres, of a style of liturgy, of a family or a community, and forget that all these are gifts given to us so that we may belong more fully to Christ. To become a fool for Christ is to let God teach us, as children are taught, and to stop measuring the things of God by the wisdom of the market, the media or the examination hall.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is teaching me, and do I let God teach me?
Point 1 · Taught by God
Listening before eating: the two tables of the Qurbana.
Point 2 · The bread of life
The manna that kept bodies alive, and the bread that conquers death.
Point 3 · You belong to Christ
No party, no preacher, no human boast: all is ours, and we are Christ's.
Take-home line
“I am the bread of life.”
live: Let God teach you (John 6:45)
Read the Gospel of Sunday's Qurbana at home before you go, so that you come to the table of the Word ready to listen.
Do not boast about human leaders (1 Corinthians 3:21)
If you have taken sides in a quarrel about preachers, priests or movements in your parish, make peace with someone on the other side.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Father teaches us by drawing us to the Son. Do not seek a teacher on earth who could lead you to God apart from Christ; the Master is within, and those who are taught by the Father come to the Son as the hungry come to bread.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Paul does not tell the wise to give up their minds, but to give up the wisdom that is puffed up. Become a fool for Christ, that is, let him teach you, and then you will truly be wise; for the one who will not learn as a child will never learn at all.
magis: Catechism 1346

The liturgy of the Eucharist unfolds as one act of worship: the liturgy of the Word, with the readings and the homily, and the liturgy of the Eucharist, with the presentation of the gifts, the consecration and Communion.
Catechism 1094
It is in the harmony of the two Testaments that the paschal catechesis of the Lord is built; the manna in the desert prefigures the Eucharist, the true bread from heaven.
Catechism 153
Faith is a gift of God, a supernatural virtue infused by him; Jesus says that this revelation does not come from flesh and blood but from the Father who is in heaven.
saints: This week

26–31 May: second and third weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles. 2027-05-28.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you alone have seen the Father, and you make him known to us. Teach us, as the prophets promised, so that we may hear and learn from the Father and come to you. You are the bread of life: give us faith to receive you, and life that death cannot end. Deliver us from the wisdom of this world that is foolishness with God, from boasting and from divisions, and keep us always yours, as you are the Father's. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Every Holy Qurbana sets two tables before us: the table of the Word, where God teaches us, and the table of the Body and Blood, where the bread of life is given. Let us listen at the first so that we may receive at the second with faith.

2027-05-29.title: Second Saturday of the Apostles
2027-05-29.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Sharing in the Body of Christ
2027-05-29.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of St Paul VI, pope.
2027-05-29.verse: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
theo: All week the readings have followed the sixth chapter of John; today, at the end of the week of the Body and Blood of Christ, we go back to its beginning, the sign that opened the whole discourse. A large crowd follows Jesus to the far side of the Sea of Galilee, and John notes that “the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near.” The feeding is a Passover sign, pointing to the new Passover of the Last Supper. Jesus asks Philip, “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” He asks it, John says, to test him, “for he himself knew what he was going to do.” Philip does the arithmetic: “Six months’ wages would not buy enough bread for each of them to get a little.” Andrew finds a boy: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?” Barley loaves were the bread of the poor. The boy gives what he has, and it is not enough, and Jesus does not ask for more. He takes it, gives thanks and distributes it, and some five thousand eat “as much as they wanted.” The words are the words of the Eucharist: he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them. Every Holy Qurbana begins with our small offering, bread and wine and the gifts of the faithful, and the Lord does with it far more than we could imagine.

Two details are easy to miss. First: “When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, ‘Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.’ So they gathered them up, and … they filled twelve baskets.” The Lord who gives in abundance does not waste. The twelve baskets, one for each apostle, are carried by the Twelve; they will feed the twelve tribes of a new Israel with what the Lord has blessed. And the words “so that nothing may be lost” echo what Jesus says later in the chapter about people: “that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39). Second: when the crowd wants to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdraws to the mountain alone. He will not be a king who wins votes with bread. His kingship will be revealed on the Cross, and the bread he will give is his own flesh.

Paul draws the conclusion for a Church living among many altars. Corinth was full of temples, and meat sacrificed to idols was sold in the market and served at banquets. Paul writes: “Therefore, my dear friends, flee from the worship of idols.” Then he gives the reason: “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.” The word translated sharing is koinonia, communion. Holy Communion is not a private devotion between me and Jesus; it makes us one body. That is why Paul says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.” He is not scorning the neighbours of the Corinthians; he is warning Christians against a divided heart. Our idols today are rarely made of stone or metal. They are money and success, the craving for approval, trust in charms and lucky days in place of trust in God. Whoever has eaten the one bread cannot give the heart to them. And whoever has eaten the one bread cannot ignore the hungry: the bread we break at the altar sends us to break our bread with the poor, and to gather up the fragments, so that nothing and no one is lost.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is my five loaves and two fish, and have I given it?
Point 1 · Five barley loaves
The boy's small gift, and the Lord who takes, gives thanks and distributes.
Point 2 · So that nothing may be lost
Twelve baskets, and the king who withdraws to the mountain.
Point 3 · One bread, one body
Communion that makes us one, and the divided heart.
Take-home line
“We who are many are one body.”
live: Give your five loaves (John 6:9)
Offer the Lord one small, concrete gift this week: an hour, a talent, a sum of money for someone in need.
Gather up the fragments (John 6:12)
Waste no food at home this week; share what is left over with someone who needs it.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Lord who multiplied the five loaves is the same who every year multiplies a few seeds into whole harvests. Because that wonder happens every day, we have stopped marvelling at it; so he did on the mountain in an hour what he does in the fields in a year, that we might wake up and praise the Creator.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

You honour the Body of Christ at the altar with silk vestments; do not despise him when he is naked in the poor. What use is it to load his table with golden cups if he himself is dying of hunger? First feed the hungry, then adorn the altar with what remains.
magis: Catechism 1335

The miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord said the blessing, broke and distributed the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigure the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist.
Catechism 1396
The unity of the Mystical Body: the Eucharist makes the Church. Those who receive the Eucharist are united more closely to Christ, and Christ unites them to all the faithful in one body.
Catechism 1397
The Eucharist commits us to the poor. To receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren.
saints: Today

Latin calendar: St Paul VI (1897–1978), pope from 1963 to 1978, who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close. In December 1964 he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope to visit India. On Saturdays, and in this last week of May, we also turn to the Mother of God.
This week

26–31 May: second and third weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Wed 26: in the Latin calendar, St Philip Neri. Thu 27: the Feast of the Body and Blood of Christ (the Latin Church in India keeps Corpus Christi on Sunday 30 May). Sat 29: in the Latin calendar, St Paul VI. Sun 30: Third Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 31: the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which closes the month of Mary. The Sacred Heart of Jesus falls on Friday 4 June.
2027-05-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you took the boy's five barley loaves, gave thanks and fed the multitude, and you told your disciples to gather the fragments so that nothing might be lost. Take the little we have and make it enough for others. You are the one bread that makes us one body: keep our hearts undivided, turned away from every idol, and open to the hungry. Through the prayers of Mary, your Mother, who gave you flesh, make us faithful to the table of the Lord. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the offertory of the Holy Qurbana the Church brings bread and wine, our five loaves and two fish. The Lord takes them, gives thanks and makes them his Body and Blood, the one bread that makes us one body.

2027-05-31.title: Third Monday of the Apostles · The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
2027-05-31.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-05-31.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary is listed in the First Set calendar as an important Marian feast, with the readings above. Weekday readings of the Third Monday of the Apostles: 1 Corinthians 12:18–27; John 6:30–36. The Latin Church keeps the feast of the Visitation on the same day. Today the month of Mary (May devotion) comes to its close in many parishes and homes (verify locally which readings are used).
2027-05-31.verse: And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
theo: On the last day of the month of Mary the Church follows her on a journey. Luke has just told of the Annunciation: the angel has left, the Word has become flesh in her womb, and she has heard that her elderly kinswoman Elizabeth, who was called barren, is in her sixth month. Mary does not stay at home to guard her secret. “In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country.” It was a long journey, perhaps four or five days on foot from Nazareth to the hill country of Judea, which tradition places at Ain Karem near Jerusalem. The haste is not anxiety; it is the haste of love and of joy. St Ambrose says that she went joyful in her desire, devout in her duty, eager in her gladness. The first thing Mary does after receiving Christ is to carry him to someone who needs her. That is the pattern of every Christian life, and especially of this Season of the Apostles: the one who has received Christ goes out in haste to bring him to others. Pope Francis took Mary's haste as the theme of the World Youth Day at Lisbon in 2023, “Mary arose and went with haste”, and told the young that it is the haste of one who cannot keep a great gift to herself.

Then the meeting: Mary “entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and exclaimed with a loud cry, ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?’” Two women meet, one old and one young, both carrying a child that only God could give. But the real meeting is between the two children: John, still unborn, leaps for joy before the unborn Christ. The Church sees here John the Baptist filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, as the angel had promised (Luke 1:15). Elizabeth's words have become our own daily prayer: in every Hail Mary we say with her, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” And she gives Mary the title that the Council of Ephesus would later solemnly proclaim: the mother of my Lord, the Mother of God.

Luke tells the story with words that recall the ark of the covenant. When King David brought the ark up to Jerusalem, he said, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); he “danced before the Lord with all his might” (2 Samuel 6:14), and the ark remained three months in the house of Obed-edom, bringing blessing. Elizabeth asks, “why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” John leaps for joy, and Mary remains with Elizabeth about three months (Luke 1:56). The Fathers and many interpreters see the meaning: Mary is the new ark, carrying not tablets of stone but the living Word of God. The Syriac Fathers, St Ephrem among them, sing of her in images like these. St John Paul II added that at the Visitation Mary became in some way the first tabernacle in history; her journey has also been called the first Eucharistic procession. How fitting that this feast falls in the week of the Body and Blood of Christ, and that the weekday Gospel today has Jesus saying, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). Mary carried the Bread of Life to Elizabeth's house; we carry him from the altar into ours.

Elizabeth's last word is a beatitude, the first in Luke's Gospel: “And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.” Mary is blessed first not because of a privilege, but because she believed. She is the model of faith for every disciple. And from that faith comes love in action, which is what Paul describes in the Epistle chosen for the feast: “Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good; love one another with mutual affection; outdo one another in showing honor.” Then: “Contribute to the needs of the saints; extend hospitality to strangers… Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another; do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly.” Every phrase could describe the three months at Ain Karem: a young woman who serves her older relative, rejoices with her, shares her house and her joys, and makes herself lowly though she carries the Lord. The weekday Epistle says the same in its own way: “If one member suffers, all suffer together with it; if one member is honored, all rejoice together with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26). As the month of Mary ends, the best homage we can give her is to do what she did: to believe the word of the Lord, and to set out in haste to serve someone who needs us.
conn: The ark comes to the hill country.

“How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); David “danced before the Lord with all his might” (2 Samuel 6:14); the ark remained three months in the house of Obed-edom (2 Samuel 6:11).
The feet of the messenger.
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace” (Isaiah 52:7): Mary crosses the hills of Judea carrying the Prince of Peace.
Filled with the Spirit from the womb.
The angel had said of John: “even before his birth he will be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:15).
Blessed among women.
Jael and Judith were called blessed among women for delivering Israel (Judges 5:24; Judith 13:18); Mary is blessed for the fruit of her womb, who delivers the world.
My soul magnifies the Lord.
Mary answers Elizabeth with the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), echoing the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10).
Here is your mother.
At the Cross Jesus gives his Mother to the beloved disciple: “Here is your mother” (John 19:27); the Church receives her into her own home.
altar: Mary carried the Lord in her womb to Elizabeth's house, and John leaped for joy. At the Holy Qurbana the same Lord comes to us under the forms of bread and wine; let our hearts leap like John's, and let us say with Elizabeth, “why has this happened to me, that my Lord comes to me?”
Receiving him, we become in our turn bearers of Christ. Like Mary, let us carry him in haste from the altar to those who wait for him.
outline: Opening
The last day of the month of Mary: a young woman on the road to the hill country.
Point 1 · She set out with haste
The first thing Mary does is to carry Christ to another.
Point 2 · The child leaped for joy
Two mothers, two children, and the Holy Spirit.
Point 3 · The mother of my Lord
Mary, the new ark and the first tabernacle.
Point 4 · Blessed is she who believed
Faith that becomes genuine love.
Closing image
An aunt from the hills arriving by bus with a bag of jackfruit chips and three months to give.
Take-home line
“Blessed is she who believed.”
live: Set out with haste (Luke 1:39)
Visit this week someone who needs you: an expectant mother, an elderly relative, a sick neighbour. Do not postpone it.
Pray the Hail Mary slowly (Luke 1:42)
Pray one decade of the Rosary today, pausing on Elizabeth's words in each Hail Mary.
Believe the Lord's word (Luke 1:45)
Choose one promise of God that you find hard to believe, and repeat it in prayer each day this week.
Let love be genuine (Romans 12:9–16)
Choose one phrase of today's Epistle and live it this week: hospitality, weeping with those who weep, or associating with the lowly.
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

Mary went with haste into the hill country, not as one who doubted the angel's word, but joyful in her desire, devout in her duty, eager in her gladness. The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow efforts. Elizabeth heard the voice first, but John felt the grace first.
St Ambrose (in substance)

Let the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord; let the spirit of Mary be in each of us to rejoice in God. According to the flesh there is one mother of Christ, but according to faith Christ is the fruit of all who believe.
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)

She who was raised by grace above all others remained humble. Mary does not glory in herself but in God her Saviour, and so teaches us that those who receive great gifts must give the more thanks and keep themselves the more lowly.
magis: Catechism 495

Called in the Gospels the mother of Jesus, Mary is acclaimed by Elizabeth, at the prompting of the Spirit, even before the birth of her son, as the mother of my Lord; the Church confesses that Mary is truly Mother of God (Theotokos).
Catechism 717
John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb; by the Spirit, Elizabeth was blessed with the visit of Mary.
Catechism 148
The Virgin Mary most perfectly embodies the obedience of faith; that is why Elizabeth greets her: Blessed is she who believed.
Catechism 2676
The second part of the Hail Mary takes up Elizabeth's greeting: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.
St John Paul II, Ecclesia de Eucharistia 55
When, at the Visitation, Mary bore in her womb the Word made flesh, she became in some way a tabernacle, the first tabernacle in history.
saints: Today
The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, an important Marian feast in the First Set calendar, kept on the same day in the Latin calendar. Close of the month of Mary.
Next days
Fri 4 June: the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Third Friday of the Apostles). Sun 6 June: Fourth Sunday of the Apostles.
2027-05-31.prayer: Lord God, you inspired the Blessed Virgin Mary, carrying your Son in her womb, to set out in haste to visit Elizabeth, and at her greeting John leaped for joy and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. Give us Mary's faith, to believe that your word will be fulfilled, and her haste, to carry Christ to those who need him. Make our love genuine, our homes hospitable and our hearts lowly. As we close this month of Mary, keep us under her protection, and let us magnify you with her all our days. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

quick: Isaiah: how beautiful are the feet of the messenger of peace; all the ends of the earth shall see God's salvation.
Acts: Peter's vision: what God has made clean, you must not call profane.
Ephesians: Christ is our peace; he has broken down the dividing wall.
John: Jesus prays that all may be one, so that the world may believe.
2027-05-02.action: Pray every day this week for Christian unity, and reach out to someone your circle keeps at a distance.
2027-05-02.question: Which dividing wall am I still keeping standing in my heart or my community?
catechism: The unity of the Church and the call to unity.
The Church and the Jewish people.
The Eucharist makes the Church one.
kidsaint: St Athanasius

Athanasius was a bishop in Egypt long ago. Some people said that Jesus was not truly God. Athanasius said: Jesus is truly God and truly man! Because of this he was sent away from his city five times. He never gave up. His feast is today, 2 May, but this year Sunday comes first.
2027-05-02.special: Sixth Sunday of Resurrection. The Ascension on Thursday 6 May.
term: Ecumenism

The movement of prayer, dialogue and common work for the unity of all Christians, which the Catholic Church embraced at the Second Vatican Council in answer to Jesus' prayer “that they may all be one” (John 17:21).

family.explain: Before he died, Jesus prayed for his friends. He also prayed for us! He asked the Father that all who believe in him would be one, like one big family. When we fight and stay angry, it makes Jesus sad. When we forgive and play together, it shows the world that Jesus is real.
family.intention: We pray for all Christians, that they may love one another and be united.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone in our family or class we need to make peace with this week?”

illus: An illustration

In a parish in central Kerala, two families had not spoken to each other for eleven years because of a boundary wall between their properties. Both came to the same Sunday Qurbana and sat on opposite sides of the church. One year, on the Sunday when the Gospel of Jesus' prayer for unity was read, the vicar asked each family in his homily to think of one wall in their lives. That afternoon the older of the two men walked to his neighbour's gate. ‘The wall can stay,’ he said, ‘but I want my grandchildren to grow up knowing your grandchildren.’ The two families were seen walking to church together the following Sunday.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you prayed that we may all be one. Gather us now in your Spirit, break down what divides us, and make us one family in you. Amen. Alleluia!
share: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace (Isaiah 52:7). To whom can I bring good news this week?
What God has made clean, you must not call profane (Acts 10:15). Whom have I judged or kept at a distance?
He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Where do I need Christ's peace in my family or community?
That they may all be one (John 17:21). How can I help to build unity among Christians?
pm.resp: Lord, make us one in you.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a sign of unity for all the nations.
For the unity of all Christians, especially the Churches of the St Thomas tradition in India.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may grow in love of his name and faithfulness to his covenant.
For our society, that walls of caste, religion and wealth may be broken down.
For our families and parish, that we may forgive one another and live as one household.
pm.close: Father, through the blood of your Son you have brought near those who were far off. Make us one, as you and your Son are one, so that the world may believe. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

quick: 2 Kings: Elijah is taken up; Elisha sees him go and receives a double share of his spirit.
Acts: as they were watching, he was lifted up; you will be my witnesses to the ends of the earth; he will come again in the same way.
1 Timothy: one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human; pray for everyone.
Luke: lifting up his hands, he blessed them and was carried up into heaven; they returned with great joy.
2027-05-06.action: Take part in the Holy Qurbana of the Ascension today, and begin a novena to the Holy Spirit tomorrow with your family.
2027-05-06.question: Do I live as one whose Head is already in heaven, or only with my eyes on the earth?
catechism: He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.
kidsaint: St Dominic Savio

Dominic was an Italian boy who studied at the school of St John Bosco. He wanted to be a saint while he was still young. He was kind to the boys others teased, he stopped fights, and he loved to visit Jesus in the church. He died when he was only fourteen. His feast is today, 6 May, but this year the Ascension of Jesus comes first.
2027-05-06.special: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD. Sixth Thursday of Resurrection. Day of obligation.
term: Sullaqa

The Syriac name of the feast of the Ascension, meaning ‘the going up’; in the West Syriac pronunciation used by the Malankara Church, Suloko. Our Church keeps it on the fortieth day after Easter as a Feast of Our Lord and a day of obligation.

family.explain: Forty days after he rose from the dead, Jesus took his friends to a hill. He lifted up his hands and blessed them, and then he went up into heaven, and a cloud hid him. His friends were not sad! They were full of joy, because they knew Jesus is with the Father and still with them. Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit, so they went back and prayed with Mary, waiting.
family.intention: We pray that the Holy Spirit will come into our family, and we begin to wait for Pentecost with Mary.
family.ask: Ask: “What can we do together each evening until Pentecost to prepare for the Holy Spirit?”

illus: An illustration

An old fisherman in Alappuzha used to see off his son each year at Kochi airport when the young man went back to his job abroad. One year his grandson, about six years old, cried as the plane took off. The old man picked him up and said, ‘Don't cry. Your father has gone ahead to make a place ready. Every month he will send what we need, and one day he will bring you there too.’ The boy's mother said later that she thought of that moment every year on the Ascension. Christ has gone ahead, not away. He sends us the gift of the Spirit, and one day he will take us where he is. Like every human picture, it falls short: no plane carries Christ away from us; he is with us always.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, ascended into heaven, lift up your hands over us and bless us, as you blessed your apostles. Fill us with great joy as we gather in your name. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit (2 Kings 2:9). What do I ask of the Lord as I prepare for Pentecost?
Why do you stand looking up toward heaven? (Acts 1:11). Where am I passive when the Lord wants me to act?
There is also one mediator between God and humankind (1 Timothy 2:5). For whom do I need to pray today?
They returned to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:52). What gives me joy in this feast?
